question: Y1
answer:
ANSWER

10 years. A manufacturer must keep the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of the national authorities for 10 years after the measuring instrument has been placed on the market. The same 10-year period applies to both documents; the Directive does not set different periods for the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity.

1. LEGAL BASIS (Directive 2014/32/EU)

1.1 Primary obligation - Article 17(3) (Obligations of manufacturers):
"Manufacturers shall keep the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years after the measuring instrument has been placed on the market."

1.2 Corroborating provisions in the Annexes, all using the same 10-year period:
- Annex II, point 5.2: "The manufacturer shall draw up a written EU declaration of conformity for each instrument model and keep it at the disposal of the national authorities for 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market. ... A copy of the EU declaration of conformity shall be made available to the relevant authorities upon request. A copy ... shall be supplied with each measuring instrument that is placed on the market. However, this requirement may be interpreted as applying to a batch or consignment rather than individual instruments in those cases where a large number of instruments is delivered to a single user."
- Annex II, point 6: "The manufacturer shall, for a period ending 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market, keep at the disposal of the national authorities: (a) the documentation referred to in point 3.1; (b) the information relating to the change referred to in point 3.5, as approved; (c) the decisions and reports from the notified body referred to in points 3.5, 4.3 and 4.4." (the quality-system variant of point 6 adds "(b) the documentation concerning the quality system referred to in point 3.1").
- Module B (EU-type examination): "The manufacturer shall keep a copy of the EU-type examination certificate, its annexes and additions together with the technical documentation at the disposal of the national authorities for 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market."
- Other module annexes use the same formula, e.g. "The manufacturer shall keep the technical documentation at the disposal of the national authorities for 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market"; "... keep the technical documentation at the disposal of the relevant national authorities for 10 years ..."; "... keep the certificates of conformity at the disposal of the national authorities for 10 years ..."; and, for the module that pairs the DoC with the technical file, "... keep it together with the technical documentation at the disposal of the national authorities for 10 years after the instrument has been placed on the market."
- Authorised representative - Article 19(1)(a): the written mandate must allow the authorised representative at least to "keep the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation at the disposal of national market surveillance authorities for 10 years after the measuring instrument has been placed on the market". Appointment of an authorised representative does not shorten or shift the manufacturer's own 10-year duty.

1.3 Sources used: EUR-Lex CELEX 32014L0032 (both the TXT and ELI/oj/eng renderings, fetched 2026-11-22) and the adopted text of Annex II on legislation.gov.uk (fetched 2026-11-22). The Commission's summary page for 32014L0032, fetched 2026-11-22, restates the rule: manufacturers "(and, if one is appointed, an authorised representative) keep the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity ... for 10 years after the MI has been placed on the market".

2. WHICH TEXT IS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21

- Directive 2014/32/EU was to be transposed by 19 April 2016 and its rules apply from 20 April 2016.
- Directive (EU) 2026/706 (OJ L, 20.3.2026) amends Directive 2014/32/EU. It entered into force on the twentieth day following publication (approximately 9 April 2026), must be transposed by 10 April 2028, and its new rules apply from 10 October 2028. It extends scope to measuring systems for electric vehicle supply equipment and for compressed gas dispensers and updates requirements for gas meters/conversion devices, active electrical energy meters and thermal energy meters (including cooling).
- Therefore, on 2026-11-21 the amending Directive is in force but its substantive rules are not yet applicable. The obligations actually binding on a manufacturer on that date are those of Directive 2014/32/EU as transposed into national law, i.e. the text quoted in section 1.
- Even on the assumption that 2026/706 altered the retention clause (nothing in the fetched material suggests it does; the Commission summary updated for 2026/706 still says 10 years), the alteration could not bite before 10 October 2028 and so could not change the answer for 2026-11-21. On the correct reading, the figure is 10 years before and after the amendment.
- The transitional provisions in Article 2 of 2026/706 (making available / putting into use of instruments conforming on 8 April 2026 and placed on the market before 10 October 2028; the Annexes Va/VIIa derogation with a 10 April 2030 cut-off; validity of certificates until 10 April 2038) concern market access and certificate validity. None of them alters the documentation-retention period. Note that 10 April 2028, 10 October 2028, 10 April 2030 and 10 April 2038 are calendar dates in those transitional rules - they are not retention periods and must not be read as such.

3. HOW THE 10 YEARS IS COMPUTED

3.1 Trigger event: the date on which the individual instrument is placed on the market - i.e. the first making available of that instrument on the Union market in the course of a commercial activity. It is not the date of manufacture, not the date the EU declaration of conformity was signed, not the date of notified-body certification, and not the date of putting into use (first use by the end user for its intended purpose). Where an instrument is imported from a third country, the clock starts with its first making available on the Union market, not with the export or manufacture date.
(Note: the Article 2 definitions of 'placing on the market', 'making available on the market' and 'putting into use' were not among the passages retrieved; they are the standard NLF-derived definitions and should be confirmed against Article 2 of the consolidated text before being quoted verbatim in a legal notice.)

3.2 The period runs per instrument, not per model or per production batch. A production run placed on the market over several months generates a rolling set of expiry dates, one per serial number.

3.3 Calculation: expiry = date placed on the market + 10 years (the tenth anniversary). Worked example: an instrument placed on the market on 2026-11-21 must be retained until 2036-11-21. Because the Directive does not state whether the day of placing on the market counts as day one, a conservative retention rule should keep records to the end of the anniversary year (here 31 December 2036) or apply an internal buffer of one calendar quarter beyond the anniversary.

3.4 The obligation is a minimum. National transposing law, sector-specific metrology rules, or other Union or national law (e.g. general product-safety or contractual/limitation rules) may require longer retention; the Directive does not prohibit keeping records longer.

4. WHAT EXACTLY MUST BE KEPT

For 10 years after placing on the market, at the disposal of the national (market surveillance) authorities:
(a) the technical documentation referred to in Annex II point 3.1 (and the equivalent point in the applicable module annex) - the documentation permitting assessment of the instrument's conformity with the essential requirements in Annex I and the relevant instrument-specific annex;
(b) the EU declaration of conformity, drawn up per instrument model, identifying the model for which it was drawn up;
(c) module-dependent records: the EU-type examination certificate with its annexes and additions (module B); approved changes notified under point 3.5; the decisions and reports of the notified body under points 3.5, 4.3 and 4.4; where the quality-system route is used, the quality-system documentation referred to in point 3.1; and certificates of conformity where a module requires them.

Form: the Directive requires the documents to be kept "at the disposal" of the authorities; retention in electronic form is acceptable provided a legible copy can be produced on request. Information and documentation supplied to a national authority on reasoned request must be in paper or electronic form and in a language easily understood by that authority.

5. WHO CARRIES THE DUTY

- Manufacturer: the 10-year retention duty in Article 17(3) is the manufacturer's, and it is not discharged by appointing an authorised representative.
- Authorised representative: if one is appointed by written mandate, the mandate must include keeping the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation at the disposal of the market surveillance authorities for 10 years after placing on the market (Article 19(1)(a)).
- Importers: the Directive places a parallel duty on importers to keep a copy of the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of the market surveillance authorities for 10 years after placing on the market and to ensure the technical documentation can be made available on request. (This mirrors the standard NLF importer obligation; the precise article number in Directive 2014/32/EU should be confirmed against the consolidated text before being cited.)
- Distributors: no independent 10-year documentation-retention duty of the same kind, but they must be able to identify who supplied them and to whom they supplied, and must cooperate with market surveillance.

6. EDGE CASES

6.1 Instruments placed on the market before 20 April 2016: Directive 2014/32/EU does not apply retroactively; retention for those instruments is governed by the preceding national rules (in the UK/IE context historically, the 2004 measuring-instruments regulations or the earlier national metrology regime). The 10-year rule applies to instruments placed on the market from 20 April 2016 onwards.
6.2 Second-hand instruments imported into the Union: they are 'new to the Union market' and their first making available in the Union starts the 10-year clock, even though they are not newly manufactured.
6.3 Instruments covered by the 2026/706 transition (EVSE, compressed gas dispensers placed on the market under national rules before 10 April 2030): retention during the transitional window follows the national rules under which they were placed on the market; the amended 10-year rule applies once the amended Directive governs the placing on the market.
6.4 Expiry of the period does not make an instrument lawful if it is non-compliant, and does not extinguish market surveillance powers under other provisions; it only ends the specific Article 17(3) retention duty.
6.5 The obligation is uniform across all instrument categories covered by the Directive (water meters, gas meters and conversion devices, active electrical energy meters, thermal energy meters, measuring systems for continuous and dynamic measurement of quantities of liquids other than water, automatic weighing instruments, taximeters, material measures, dimensional measuring instruments). No instrument-specific annex sets a different retention period.

7. COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE (implementation-ready)

7.1 Maintain a documentation-retention register with, per instrument serial number (or per model plus serial range where serialised tracking is impractical): model/type; notified-body certificate reference; date placed on the market (first making available in the Union); retention expiry date (= placing-on-market date + 10 years); document location/identifier for the technical file and the DoC; language versions held; review/expiry owner.
7.2 On each placing on the market event, create the retention record automatically as part of the shipping/release step, and set an expiry reminder 90 days before the tenth anniversary so that no record is destroyed early by routine housekeeping.
7.3 Apply a destruction hold: no deletion of technical files or DoCs without a check that the tenth anniversary of placing on the market has passed (and that no national rule, claim, investigation or recall requires longer retention).
7.4 Keep the DoC retrievable by model, since the Article 17(3)/Annex II point 5.2 duty is framed per instrument model, and keep the technical file retrievable by instrument so that a request naming a single serial number can be answered.
7.5 On a reasoned request from a national authority, produce the documents in paper or electronic form, in a language easily understood by that authority, within the period the authority sets; the 10-year retention duty exists precisely to make this possible.
7.6 If an authorised representative is appointed, record the mandate clause implementing Article 19(1)(a) and confirm the representative in fact holds the DoC and technical documentation for the full 10 years (the manufacturer's own duty remains).

8. VERIFICATION NOTES

- The 10-year figure is confirmed by three independent renderings of the Directive's text (EUR-Lex CELEX TXT, EUR-Lex ELI/OJ, legislation.gov.uk adopted Annex II) and by the Commission's summary page updated for Directive (EU) 2026/706.
- Two points are stated on the basis of the Directive's standard NLF architecture rather than a retrieved quotation and should be confirmed against the consolidated text before being relied on in a legal notice: (i) the Article 2 definitions of 'placing on the market' / 'making available on the market' / 'putting into use'; (ii) the exact article number of the importer's 10-year DoC retention duty.
- The ask numbered 1 contains an unfilled placeholder ('[constraint]'); no constraint has been applied. The identifier supplied for it records the version determination only.

question: Y2
answer:
SCOPE OF DIRECTIVE 2014/35/EU (LOW VOLTAGE DIRECTIVE) — VOLTAGE-RATING BANDS, AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21, ANNEX II EXCLUSIONS SET ASIDE

1. ANSWER

The Directive applies to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of:

- Alternating current (AC): from 50 V up to and including 1 000 V.
- Direct current (DC): from 75 V up to and including 1 500 V.

Outside those bands the Directive does not apply by its own terms, whether or not the equipment appears in any exclusion list.

Tabulated:

| Current | Lower limit (in scope at and above) | Upper limit (in scope at and below) |
|---|---|---|
| AC | 50 V | 1 000 V |
| DC | 75 V | 1 500 V |

2. LEGAL BASIS (operative text)

Directive 2014/35/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2016 on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of electrical equipment designed for use within certain voltage limits (recast), OJ L 96, 29.3.2014, p. 357–374; CELEX 32014L0035; consolidated CELEX 02014L0035. Applicable since 20 April 2016 (repealing Directive 2006/95/EC).

Article 1(1) — Scope:

"This Directive shall apply to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 and 1 000 V for alternating current and between 75 and 1 500 V for direct current."

Article 1(2) then removes from scope the equipment and areas of use listed in Annex II (the exclusions the request asks to be set aside; they are not itemised here).

Terminology point (the plan flagged 'nominal'): the operative term in Article 1(1) is "voltage rating", not "nominal voltage". The 50/1 000 V and 75/1 500 V figures are frequently paraphrased in secondary sources as "nominal" limits; that paraphrase is acceptable shorthand but the test to apply is the equipment's voltage rating. Harmonised-standard definitions (e.g. standard-voltage series) do not enlarge or narrow Article 1(1).

3. BOUNDARY AND INTERPRETATION RULES (apply these before any exclusion analysis)

3.1 Inclusive limits. Article 1(1) reads "between … and …". Treat both ends as inclusive: equipment rated exactly 50 V AC or exactly 1 000 V AC, and exactly 75 V DC or exactly 1 500 V DC, is inside the scope bands. 49 V AC / 74 V DC and 1 001 V AC / 1 501 V DC are outside. Borderline ratings should be checked against the Commission's LVD Guide before a scope decision is recorded.

3.2 "Voltage rating" means the rating the manufacturer declares for the equipment (nameplate, marking, instructions) — i.e. the input/output/service voltage for which the equipment is designed. It is not the internal operating voltage of the electronics, nor the supply voltage of the installation, nor a transient/overvoltage-category figure. A 230 V AC appliance containing 5 V logic is in scope on the strength of its 230 V AC rating.

3.3 Multiple or ranged ratings. Where equipment carries more than one rating (e.g. 100–240 V AC, or 230 V AC / 12 V DC), assess each rating against the bands. If any rating lies inside a band, the equipment is within Article 1(1) scope. Equipment whose declared range straddles a limit (e.g. 24–400 V AC) is in scope, because it is designed for use at voltages inside the band.

3.4 Three-phase equipment. Rate on the declared voltage, normally the line-to-line voltage. A 400/690 V AC three-phase product is in scope (690 V ≤ 1 000 V AC).

3.5 The bands are current-specific. An AC rating is tested against 50–1 000 V and a DC rating against 75–1 500 V; do not convert one into the other to move a product in or out of scope.

3.6 Components. The Directive addresses "electrical equipment" made available on the market. A component supplied solely for incorporation into other equipment is not, on its own, the subject of the LVD conformity obligations; once incorporated, the assembly's rating governs. Components placed on the market as finished products for end users are assessed on their own rating.

4. RELATIONSHIP TO THE ANNEX II EXCLUSIONS (constraint 3)

4.1 The two tests are sequential and independent:

- Step 1 (Article 1(1)): is the voltage rating inside the bands? If no, the Directive does not apply and no exclusion analysis is needed.
- Step 2 (Article 1(2)/Annex II): if yes, is the equipment or area of use listed in Annex II? If yes, the Directive does not apply.

4.2 Annex II exclusions are voltage-independent: equipment listed there is out of scope even at, say, 230 V AC. Conversely, equipment not listed in Annex II is still out of scope if its rating falls outside the bands.

4.3 Per the request, the Annex II items are not enumerated or analysed here; they are set aside. Nothing in the exclusion list alters the figures in section 1.

5. SCOPE-DECISION PROCEDURE (repeatable checklist)

1. Identify every declared voltage rating of the equipment (AC and DC separately) from marking, datasheet and instructions. Record the source document.
2. For each AC rating Ur(AC): inside if 50 ≤ Ur(AC) ≤ 1 000 V. For each DC rating Ur(DC): inside if 75 ≤ Ur(DC) ≤ 1 500 V.
3. If no rating is inside either band → equipment is outside the LVD by Article 1(1). Record 'out of scope — below/above voltage limits' and consider other Union law (e.g. General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988, EMC Directive 2014/30/EU, Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU, toy or medical-device legislation) and, for above-limit equipment, relevant national rules.
4. If at least one rating is inside a band → proceed to Annex II. If listed → out of scope by Article 1(2). If not listed → in scope; apply Articles 3–9 (safety objectives in Annex I, CE marking, EU declaration of conformity, technical documentation).
5. Record the decision, the rating relied on, and the annex/article applied, in the technical file.

6. WORKED EXAMPLES (self-check against section 1)

| Equipment | Rating relied on | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Domestic 230 V AC appliance | 230 V AC | In scope (50–1 000 V AC) unless listed in Annex II |
| 400/690 V AC three-phase assembly | 690 V AC | In scope (≤ 1 000 V AC) |
| 24 V DC LED driver / 12 V DC ITE accessory | 24 V DC / 12 V DC | Out of scope by Article 1(1) (below 75 V DC) |
| 11 kV AC switchgear | 11 000 V AC | Out of scope by Article 1(1) (above 1 000 V AC) |
| 230 V AC / 12 V DC power supply | 230 V AC | In scope (any in-band rating suffices) |
| Equipment at 230 V AC listed in Annex II | 230 V AC | Out of scope by Article 1(2), irrespective of voltage |

7. VERIFICATION STATUS OF THE 'AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21' CONSTRAINT

7.1 The figures in section 1 are the Directive's own Article 1(1) figures and are unchanged from Directive 73/23/EEC through 2006/95/EEC to 2014/35/EU. The 2014 recast changed structure, definitions and conformity-assessment mechanics, not the numerical scope limits. No amendment to Article 1(1) is known to this note.

7.2 Residual risk: an amendment entering into force on or before 2026-11-21 that alters Article 1(1). Assessed as very low (the limits are a long-settled single-market baseline), but not eliminated here: the source-retrieval step returned no extractable passage from the EUR-Lex pages consulted (CELEX 02014L0035 consolidated text, the ELI version, the summary page, the original-act page and the ELI landing page), so the consolidation could not be read and diffed. This is a retrieval limitation, not a conflict with the figures stated.

7.3 Close-out step before relying on this note in a conformity file: (a) open the EUR-Lex consolidated version of 2014/35/EU bearing the latest consolidation date on or before 2026-11-21 (CELEX 02014L0035-YYYYMMDD); (b) compare Article 1(1) word-for-word with section 2; (c) check the 'Amended by' / 'All consolidated versions' list for any act amending Article 1 or Annex II; (d) record the CELEX number and consolidation date used. If the comparison matches, this note stands unqualified; if it does not, the amended figures supersede section 1 and this note must be reissued.

7.4 Scope of the date constraint: 'as in force on 2026-11-21' is read as the Directive's own provisions, not national transpositions or harmonised standards; transposition measures cannot lawfully narrow or widen the Article 1(1) bands.

8. WHAT THIS NOTE DOES NOT DO

It does not enumerate or analyse the Annex II exclusions (set aside per the request), does not assess compliance with the Annex I safety objectives, and does not determine which harmonised standards give presumption of conformity.
cautions: The recompute vote did not run, so no figure in this answer was recomputed.
A lookup ran, but no page it named could be read, so nothing in this answer was checked against a source.

question: Y3
answer:
ANSWER

Under Regulation (EU) 2017/1369, after the final unit of a model has been placed on the market, the supplier must keep the information concerning that model in the compliance part of the product database for 15 years.

Legal basis: Article 4(6) of Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2017 setting a framework for energy labelling and repealing Directive 2010/30/EU.

VERBATIM TEXT (Article 4(6), as retrieved)

"After the final unit of a model has been placed on the market, the supplier shall keep the information concerning that model in the compliance part of the product database for a period of 15 years. Where appropriate in relation to the average life span of a product, a shorter retention period may be provided for pursuant to point (q) of Article 16(3). The information in the public part of the database shall not be deleted."

ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT READING

1. Obliged party — "the supplier", i.e. the entity that places the model on the Union market, as defined in Article 2. The duty is on the supplier, not on the dealer; dealers have separate obligations under Article 5.
2. Trigger — "after the final unit of a model has been placed on the market". The clock starts from the factual last placement on the market of a unit of that specific model, not from the last production run, not from the date the model is marked discontinued in the database, and not from the end of the calendar year.
3. Object — "the information concerning that model in the compliance part of the product database", i.e. the compliance part referred to in Article 4(7)/Article 12 (accessible only to market surveillance authorities and the Commission), containing the information set out in point 3 of Annex I, including the mandatory specific parts of the technical documentation listed in Article 12(5) (general description, references to harmonised/measurement standards, assembly/installation/maintenance/test precautions, measured technical parameters, calculations, test conditions).
4. Duration — "a period of 15 years". Rolling, per model, counted from the trigger date.
5. Carve-out — "Where appropriate in relation to the average life span of a product, a shorter retention period may be provided for pursuant to point (q) of Article 16(3)." This is a downward derogation that can only be created by a delegated act adopted under Article 16(3)(q). A supplier cannot shorten the period unilaterally, and a shorter period applies only to the product group covered by such a delegated act. Absent such an act for the product group in question, 15 years governs.
6. Counterpart rule — "The information in the public part of the database shall not be deleted." The public-part record is perpetual; the 15-year clock applies only to the compliance part.

OPERATIVE MECHANISM THE SUPPLIER MUST RUN (Article 4(4) + 4(6))

Article 4(4) requires the supplier to indicate in the database when it no longer places units of a model on the market. That indication is the evidentiary marker; the legal trigger remains the factual final placement on the market. A supplier that declares discontinuation early does not shorten the 15 years, and one that declares late does not extend it — but a late declaration is itself an Article 4(4) non-compliance and will look like an Article 4(6) retention failure in an audit, so the two must be run together.

COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE

Step 1 — Model-level register. Maintain, per model identifier (and per equivalent model grouping), a record with: model identifier; delegated act(s) covering it; EPREL registration date; date of first placement on the market; date of final placement on the market; source evidence for that date; calculated retention end date (= date of final placement + 15 years); any applicable Article 16(3)(q) shorter period with the delegated act citation.

Step 2 — Fix the trigger date on evidence. Acceptable evidence of the final placement: last invoice/dispatch note to a distributor or dealer in the Union, last transfer-of-ownership document, customs release record for the last consignment, or a written confirmation from the distribution chain that no further units remain available on the market. Do not use the end-of-production date as a proxy unless it coincides.

Step 3 — Enter the discontinuation indication in the database at the point the final unit is placed on the market (Article 4(4)), and record the same date in the register.

Step 4 — Calculate and diary the retention end date. Retention end = trigger date + 15 years. Example: final unit placed on the market 2026-11-21 → compliance-part retention runs to 2041-11-21.

Step 5 — Do not delete from the public part, ever. On expiry of the compliance-part period, remove/close the compliance-part record only; the public-part information stays (Article 4(6), third sentence).

Step 6 — Check for a product-specific shorter period before applying 15 years. Consult the delegated act(s) adopted for that product group under Article 16(3)(q). If one specifies a shorter period by reference to average product life span, apply that shorter period and cite the act in the register; otherwise apply 15 years. Where a shorter period applies, the public-part non-deletion rule is unaffected.

Step 7 — Retention of the evidence itself. The 15-year duty covers the information in the compliance part; keep the trigger-date evidence for at least the same period so the calculation can be defended in a market surveillance check.

Step 8 — Change control. If a model is modified in a way relevant to the label or the product information sheet, Article 4(4) makes it a new model — open a new register line with its own trigger date and its own 15-year clock; do not let the successor model inherit the predecessor's end date.

Step 9 — Periodic review. Annual reconciliation of the register against ERP/dispatch data to confirm no model has passed its trigger date without a discontinuation indication and a diary entry.

VERSION CONTROL FOR THE 2026-11-21 SNAPSHOT

The Article 4(6) wording above was retrieved twice from independent page renderings of the regulation (the Article 4 page and the whole-body page), with identical text, and nothing in the retrieved material records any amendment to Article 4(6). Residual verification step before this answer is relied on formally: confirm against the EUR-Lex consolidated version of Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 (CELEX 02017R1369) generated for 2026-11-21, checking (a) that Article 4(6) still reads "15 years", and (b) whether any delegated act adopted under Article 16(3)(q) has introduced a shorter period for the specific product group concerned. Neither check is expected to change the framework answer of 15 years; the second can only shorten it for a specific group.

COMMON ERRORS THIS ANSWER IS MEANT TO PREVENT

- Confusing the compliance part (15 years, then deletable) with the public part (never deleted).
- Running the clock from the end of production or from the discontinuation declaration instead of the final placement on the market.
- Applying a shorter period without a delegated act under Article 16(3)(q) authorising it for that product group.
- Treating a label/product-information-sheet-relevant change as a continuation of the old model rather than a new model under Article 4(4).

OUTSIDE THIS FUNCTION

National implementing measures, contractual retention duties owed to distributors, and the mechanics of the EPREL data-entry interface are not determined by Article 4(6) and are not answered here; they should be checked separately against applicable national law and the Commission's EPREL guidance.

question: Y4
answer:
ANSWER

Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/1189, Annex II, point 1(c), as applicable on 2026-11-21:

| Boiler type | Seasonal space heating PM emission limit |
|---|---|
| Automatically stoked solid fuel boiler | not higher than 40 mg/m3 |
| Manually stoked solid fuel boiler | not higher than 60 mg/m3 |

Operative wording (Annex II, point 1, opening sentence: 'From 1 January 2020 solid fuel boilers shall comply with the following requirements:'):

  '(c) seasonal space heating emissions of particulate matter shall not be higher than 40 mg/m3 for automatically stoked boilers and not be higher than 60 mg/m3 for manually stoked boilers;'

and the closing sentence of Annex II point 1: 'These requirements shall be met for the preferred fuel and for any other suitable fuel for the solid fuel boiler.'

1. WHAT THE NUMBER MEANS (do not quote 40/60 without this)

1.1 Metric. 'Seasonal space heating emissions' is defined in Annex I(1) as a mg/m3 figure built as follows:
  (a) automatically stoked solid fuel boilers: weighted average of emissions at rated heat output and at 30 % of rated heat output;
  (b) manually stoked boilers that can be operated at 50 % of rated heat output in continuous mode: weighted average of emissions at rated heat output and at 50 % of rated heat output;
  (c) manually stoked boilers that cannot be operated at 50 % or less of rated heat output in continuous mode: the emissions at rated heat output only;
  (d) solid fuel cogeneration boilers: the emissions at rated heat output only.

1.2 Calculation (Annex III, point 6(b)):
  Es = 0,85 x Es,p + 0,15 x Es,n   for automatically stoked boilers and for manually stoked boilers operable at 50 % continuously;
  Es = Es,n                        for manually stoked boilers not operable at 50 % or less continuously, and for cogeneration boilers;
  where Es,p = emission measured at 30 % or 50 % of rated heat output (as applicable) and Es,n = emission measured at rated heat output.
  Note the weighting: the part-load term carries 0,85 and the rated-load term only 0,15. A unit cannot be shown compliant on its rated-load PM figure alone.

1.3 Unit and reference conditions (Annex III, point 6(a)). PM (with OGC, CO and NOx) 'shall be expressed standardised to a dry flue gas basis at 10 % oxygen and standard conditions at 0 degC and 1 013 millibar.' So the limits are mg per cubic metre of dry flue gas at 10 % O2, 0 degC, 1013 mbar. They are NOT mg/MJ, NOT mg/Nm3 at 0 % or 3 % O2, and NOT wet-basis. Any declaration, test report or datasheet quoting 40/60 must carry the 10 % O2 / dry / 0 degC / 1013 mbar reference, otherwise the figure is misquoted.

1.4 Measurement method: PM is determined gravimetrically, excluding any particulate matter formed by organic gaseous compounds when the flue gas is mixed with ambient air (Annex III). This matters because the OGC limit (20/30 mg/m3) and the PM limit are not additive and the PM figure must not absorb condensable organic artefacts.

2. WHAT THE LIMITS DO **NOT** VARY BY (frequent error)

2.1 Rated heat output. The PM limits are a single pair of values for the whole scope (solid fuel boilers with rated heat output <= 500 kW, Article 1(1)). Unlike the energy-efficiency requirement, which is banded (>= 75 % for <= 20 kW; >= 77 % for > 20 kW, Annex II 1(a)-(b)), the PM limit is not banded by output. Do not create a 20 kW split for PM.

2.2 Fuel type. The PM limit is not split by fuel. Contrast Annex II 1(f): NOx is split (200 mg/m3 biomass boilers, 350 mg/m3 fossil fuel boilers). PM, OGC and CO are split by stoking type only. The fuel dimension enters through the 'preferred fuel and any other suitable fuel' rule: the same 40 or 60 mg/m3 must be met on the preferred fuel and on every other fuel declared suitable.

2.3 Stoking type is the only axis: automatically stoked -> 40; manually stoked -> 60. For manually stoked units, the applicable metric differs (50 % weighting vs rated-load only, see 1.1(b)/(c)) but the limit value does not: 60 mg/m3 either way.

3. STATUS 'AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21'

3.1 Instrument: Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/1189 of 28 April 2015 implementing Directive 2009/125/EC with regard to ecodesign requirements for solid fuel boilers (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L 193, 21.7.2015, p. 100. Entered into force on the twentieth day after publication (i.e. 10 August 2015). The Annex II point 1 requirements apply from 1 January 2020, so they are fully applicable on 2026-11-21.

3.2 Amendments. No amending act in force on 2026-11-21 changes the Annex II point 1(c) values; they stand as adopted in 2015. The 'changes over time' entries carried on the UK legislation.gov.uk rendering (28/04/2015; exit day 31/01/2020; end of implementation period 31/12/2020) are UK exit-related editorial versions of the same text, not amendments to the EU limits, and do not alter 40/60. Framework note: Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 (ESPR) repealed Directive 2009/125/EC, but existing implementing measures such as 2015/1189 remain in force and applicable until repealed or replaced; nothing on record replaces this measure's PM limits by 2026-11-21.

3.3 Provenance limitation (stated, not hidden). The verbatim passages available to me are from legislation.gov.uk's carriage of the EU instrument (whole regulation, Annex II, adopted-text and plain-annex views), fetched 2026-11-22, plus EUR-Lex landing pages that returned no quotable consolidated text. The Annex II text is identical across all four renders and is unamended since 2015, so the values are reliable; a declarant filing against the regulation should nevertheless cite the EUR-Lex consolidated version of 2015/1189 current on the relevant date, Annex II point 1(c), as the formal reference.

4. MARKET SURVEILLANCE TOLERANCE (do not confuse with the limit)

Annex IV (verification procedure) allows the authority to accept a determined value that exceeds the declared value by up to 2 mg/m3 for particulate matter for biomass boilers and 10 mg/m3 for fossil fuel boilers. These are check tolerances applied to the declared value; they are not alternative limits and do not permit a declared or measured seasonal-space-heating PM value above 40 / 60 mg/m3. (Annex IV also carries a 1 mg/m3 tolerance for OGC and 6 mg/m3 for CO - out of scope here, quoted only to show the tolerance block is separate from Annex II.)

5. OUT OF SCOPE FOR THIS ANSWER (listed so they are not conflated with the PM answer)

- Energy efficiency: >= 75 % (<= 20 kW) / >= 77 % (> 20 kW), Annex II 1(a)-(b).
- OGC: 20 mg/m3 auto / 30 mg/m3 manual, Annex II 1(d).
- CO: 500 mg/m3 auto / 700 mg/m3 manual, Annex II 1(e).
- NOx (as NO2): 200 mg/m3 biomass / 350 mg/m3 fossil, Annex II 1(f).
- Product information requirements (Annex II point 2) and indicative benchmarks (Annex V).

6. COMPLIANCE-ENGINEER CHECKLIST FOR APPLYING 40 / 60

6.1 Classify the unit first: automatically stoked vs manually stoked; if manually stoked, determine whether it can operate at 50 % of rated heat output in continuous mode (this selects the 0,85/0,15 weighting vs rated-load-only).
6.2 Determine every fuel declared suitable, not just the preferred fuel; the limit must be met for each.
6.3 Verify the test report states dry basis, 10 % O2, 0 degC, 1013 mbar, gravimetric PM excluding organic-condensate artefact.
6.4 Compare the computed Es (not the raw rated-load measurement) against 40 or 60 mg/m3.
6.5 Confirm the declaration carries the same reference conditions; a value presented without them is not verifiable and should be rejected at review.
6.6 Do not apply the Annex IV tolerance (2 / 10 mg/m3) at design stage - design to the limit, not to limit + tolerance.

7. SOURCES RELIED ON

- Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/1189, Annex I(1) (definition of seasonal space heating emissions), Annex II point 1(c) and closing sentence, Annex III point 6(a)-(b) (reference conditions and Es formula), Annex IV (verification tolerances), Article 1(1) (scope, <= 500 kW).
- Renders consulted (all concordant on the 40 / 60 wording): legislation.gov.uk/eur/2015/1189/2015-04-28; .../annex/II; .../annexes/adopted?view=plain; .../adopted/data.xht?view=snippet (fetched 2026-11-22).

question: Y5
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — WEEE COLLECTION RATE FROM 2019, DIRECTIVE 2012/19/EU AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21

1. ANSWER (one line)
From 2019 the minimum annual collection rate is 65 % of the average weight of electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) placed on the market in the three preceding years in the Member State concerned, or alternatively 85 % of WEEE generated on the territory of that Member State. Both figures are in Article 7(1), second subparagraph, of Directive 2012/19/EU; the two bases are alternative compliance routes, not a sequence and not a cap. The rate is still in force on 2026-11-21.

2. OPERATIVE TEXT RELIED ON (verbatim)
Article 7(1), second subparagraph, Directive 2012/19/EU:
"From 2019, the minimum collection rate to be achieved annually shall be 65 % of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years in the Member State concerned, or alternatively 85 % of WEEE generated on the territory of that Member State."
Context sentences from the same paragraph:
- First subparagraph: "From 2016, the minimum collection rate shall be 45 % calculated on the basis of the total weight of WEEE collected in accordance with Articles 5 and 6 in a given year in the Member State concerned, expressed as a percentage of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years in that Member State. Member States shall ensure that the volume of WEEE collected evolves gradually during the period from 2016 to 2019, unless the collection rate laid down in the second subparagraph has already been achieved."
- Third subparagraph: "Until 31 December 2015, a rate of separate collection of at least 4 kilograms on average per inhabitant per year of WEEE from private households or the same amount of weight of WEEE as was collected in that Member State on average in the three preceding years, whichever is greater, shall continue to apply."
- Fourth subparagraph: "Member States may set more ambitious rates for separate collection of WEEE and shall in such a case report this to the Commission."

3. COMPLIANCE RECORD (structured determination)
Obligation ID: WEEE-ART7-2019-COLLECTION-RATE
Instrument: Directive 2012/19/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) (OJ L 197, 24.7.2012, p. 38).
Provision: Article 7(1), second subparagraph (read with Article 7(2) for the evidence base and Article 5(1) for separate collection).
Addressee: each Member State (not individual producers; producer responsibility is the implementing mechanism).
Obligation type: minimum result to be achieved annually; Member States may exceed it (Art. 7(1), fourth subparagraph) and must report any more ambitious rate to the Commission.
Rate from 2019: 65 % on the placed-on-market (POM) basis, or alternatively 85 % on the WEEE-generated basis.
Frequency: annual, each calendar/reporting year, for every year from 2019 onward, including the compliance year containing 2026-11-21.
Geographic scope: territory of the Member State concerned.
Status at 2026-11-21: in force, unchanged.
Live derogations at 2026-11-21: none. The Article 7(3) derogation (Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Malta, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia: 40-45 % from 14 August 2016 and postponement of the paragraph 1 second-subparagraph rate to a date of the Member State's choice "not later than 14 August 2021") expired at the latest on 14 August 2021, i.e. before the material date. No Member State may therefore rely on it to apply less than 65 %/85 % on 2026-11-21.

4. PHASE-IN TABLE (kept separate so the from-2019 rate is not confused with earlier rates)
- Until 31 December 2015: 4 kg per inhabitant per year of WEEE from private households, or the average weight collected in the three preceding years, whichever is greater (Art. 7(1), third subparagraph).
- 2016-2018: 45 % of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years, with a gradual evolution from 2016 to 2019 unless 65 % was already achieved (Art. 7(1), first subparagraph).
- From 2019 onward (including 2026-11-21): 65 % of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years, or alternatively 85 % of WEEE generated (Art. 7(1), second subparagraph).
- No further step-up, sunset or automatic escalation exists in the Directive after the 2019 figure. 65 %/85 % is the terminal rate of Article 7 as it stands.

5. THE TWO CALCULATION BASES (the format of the answer, spelled out)
Basis A — POM basis: 65 %.
  Numerator: total weight of WEEE collected in the compliance year in the Member State in accordance with Articles 5 and 6.
  Denominator: average weight of EEE placed on the market in that Member State in the three preceding years (e.g. for compliance year 2026, the average of 2023, 2024 and 2025).
Basis B — WEEE-generated basis: 85 %.
  Numerator: same collected weight.
  Denominator: quantity of WEEE generated by weight on the territory of that Member State, determined under the common methodology for calculating WEEE generated required by Article 7(5).
Relationship: "or alternatively" — a Member State satisfies Article 7(1) by meeting either basis; they are not cumulative and neither is a ceiling. Because the denominators differ (equipment placed on the market versus waste actually arising), 85 % of generated is not a stricter or looser figure than 65 % of POM in any fixed ratio; the two are not convertible without the Article 7(5) methodology.
Supporting duties: Article 7(2) requires Member States to ensure free-of-charge transmission of information on WEEE received by collection and treatment facilities, received by distributors, and separately collected by producers or third parties on their behalf, in order to establish whether the minimum rate has been achieved.
Methodology instruments: Article 7(5) required implementing acts by 14 August 2015 establishing (a) a common methodology for calculating the weight of EEE placed on the national market and (b) a common methodology for calculating the quantity of WEEE generated by weight in each Member State. Compliance evidence must be produced on those methodologies, not on ad hoc estimates.

6. VERSION CONTROL FOR THE 2026-11-21 CONSTRAINT
- Quoted text verified against two independent renderings: the EUR-Lex consolidated text (CELEX 02012L0019; latest consolidation dated 8 April 2024, file 02012L0019-20240408) and the legislation.gov.uk rendering of Article 7 (retained EU law version, frozen at IP completion day 31 December 2020; page sha256 9ebada241f61, data page sha256 aff1f8212f61). The operative rate wording is identical in both.
- The Directive has been amended since 2012 (notably by Directive (EU) 2018/849). Those amendments did not alter the Article 7(1) rate figures: the 65 %/85 % wording appears unchanged in the post-amendment consolidated text and in the retained version.
- Article 7(4) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts laying down transitional adjustments; no such act changing the 65 %/85 % figures is in force on 2026-11-21.
- Residual verification step to be closed before relying on this determination operationally: open EUR-Lex, "All consolidated versions" and "Amendments" for CELEX 32012L0019, and confirm that no amendment adopted between 9 April 2024 and 21 November 2026 amends Article 7. On the evidence retrieved, no such amendment exists; the answer is therefore not blocked, but this check is the one control that would falsify it.
- Territorial note: the Directive binds EU Member States. The legislation.gov.uk copy is a cross-reference aid for the retained version and is not evidence of EU law after 31 December 2020; it is used here only as corroboration of the wording, which the EUR-Lex consolidation also carries. If the question is directed at GB or NI implementation, a separate national-law determination is required.

7. COMMON ERRORS THIS DETERMINATION EXCLUDES
- Stating 45 % as the from-2019 rate: 45 % is the 2016-2018 rate under Article 7(1), first subparagraph.
- Stating 4 kg/inhabitant as the current rate: that applies only until 31 December 2015.
- Stating 85 % as the headline rate: 85 % is the alternative basis (WEEE generated), not the default; 65 % on the POM basis is the primary expression.
- Treating 65 % as a ceiling: Article 7(1), fourth subparagraph, expressly permits more ambitious national rates.
- Treating the Article 7(3) transitional derogation as still available: it lapsed no later than 14 August 2021.

8. BOTTOM LINE
Minimum collection rate applicable from 2019 and in force on 2026-11-21: 65 % of the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years, or alternatively 85 % of WEEE generated on the territory of the Member State. Unit: percent. Basis: Article 7(1), second subparagraph, Directive 2012/19/EU (consolidated text CELEX 02012L0019, consolidation of 8 April 2024).

question: Y6
shape: EU ecodesign / light sources and control gear
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — Combined maximum standby / no-load power, Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/2020, as in force on 2026-11-21

1. LEGAL BASIS AND VERSION CONTROL (Ask 1 constraint)
- Instrument: Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/2020 of 1 October 2019 implementing Directive 2009/IME/EC (OJ L 315, 5.12.2019, p. 209), as corrected by corrigendum C1 (consolidated version 01.03.2021).
- Version check performed against EUR-Lex ELI/CELEX 32019R2020 (original OJ text, the 2021-03-01 consolidated text, the current consolidated text, and the legislation.gov.uk copy). Result: the two operative sentences setting the standby limit and the no-load limit read identically in every version examined — no amendment or corrigendum before 2026-11-21 alters either 0,5 W value. The C1 correction in that region of Annex II affects only the LED/OLED control-gear efficiency formula in Table 3, which is not used here.
- Applicability date: Article 3 brings the requirements into application from 1 September 2021 (Article 10 repeals Regs (EC) 244/2009, (EC) 245/2009 and (EU) 1194/2012 with effect from that date). The limits are therefore in force on 2026-11-21.
- Evidence step to keep in the compliance file: archive the EUR-Lex consolidated-text banner plus the 'All consolidated versions' list captured on or before 2026-11-21, so the version relied on is dated and auditable.

2. THE TWO LIMITS
(a) Light source — standby power. Annex II, point 1 (standby requirement for light sources): 'The standby power Psb of a light source shall not exceed 0,5 W.' Psb is defined in Article 2(27) as the electric power consumption of a light source or of a separate control gear in standby mode.
   Psb,max = 0,5 W
(b) Separate control gear — no-load power. Annex II, point 1, the paragraph immediately following Table 3 (minimum energy efficiency of separate control gears): 'The no-load power Pno of a separate control gear shall not exceed 0,5 W. This applies only to separate control gear for which the manufacturer or importer has declared in the technical documentation that it has been designed for no-load mode.' Pno is defined in Article 2(26).
   Applicability condition: the request states the control gear is 'declared for no-load mode', so the condition in the second sentence is satisfied and the 0,5 W ceiling applies.
   Pno,max = 0,5 W

3. CALCULATION
Combined maximum = Psb,max (light source) + Pno,max (separate control gear)
                = 0,500 W + 0,500 W
                = 1,000 W
Conversion: 1 W = 1 000 mW, therefore 1,000 W x 1 000 = 1 000 mW.
Exact arithmetic — no rounding is required at either step; reporting to two decimal places (1,00 W) introduces no error.

ANSWER: 1,0 W combined, which is 1000 mW.

4. QUALIFICATION OF THE FIGURE — what it is and is not (read before filing)
- The regulation sets NO combined limit. Each limit is a per-device, per-parameter ceiling: the light source is assessed against Psb <= 0,5 W and the control gear against Pno <= 0,5 W, independently. The 1,0 W figure is an arithmetic aggregation across two distinct products in the compliance file, not a regulatory threshold, and must be labelled as such in the documentation.
- The sentence 'The allowable values for Psb and Pnet shall not be added together' (Annex II, networked-standby paragraph for connected separate control gears) is NOT engaged and is NOT breached here: it forbids adding a single connected gear's standby and networked-standby allowances. This calculation adds Psb of one device to Pno of a different device. Note this explicitly in the file so a reviewer does not mistake the 1,0 W for a prohibited Psb + Pnet sum.
- Verification tolerance: Annex IV, Table 6 sets a tolerance of 0,10 W for Pno, Psb and Pnet ('the determined value shall not exceed the declared value by more than 0,10 W'). This is a market-surveillance tolerance applied to determined-versus-declared values; it does NOT raise the maximum permitted power. The maxima therefore remain 0,5 W each. A tolerance-inclusive worst case would be 0,6 W + 0,6 W = 1,2 W, but that number must never be reported as the 'maximum permitted power' — it answers a different question.
- Networked standby power Pnet (also 0,5 W) is out of scope: neither device is stated to be a connected (networked) device.

5. SUGGESTED COMPLIANCE-FILE ENTRY
| Parameter | Device | Limit | Declared | Source |
| Psb | Light source | 0,50 W | <= 0,50 W | Reg. (EU) 2019/2020, Annex II pt 1; Art. 2(27) |
| Pno | Separate control gear (declared for no-load mode) | 0,50 W | <= 0,50 W | Reg. (EU) 2019/2020, Annex II pt 1 (para. after Table 3); Art. 2(26) |
| Derived aggregate Psb + Pno | Both | not a regulatory limit | 1,00 W / 1000 mW | arithmetic sum of the two ceilings above |
Footnote to carry: '1,00 W (1000 mW) is the arithmetic sum of two independent per-device ceilings; Regulation (EU) 2019/2020 does not establish a combined limit and conformity is demonstrated separately for each parameter.'

6. ASSUMPTIONS AND CONDITIONS (state in the file; each is a scope check, not an open question)
- The light source and the separate control gear are standard products within the scope of Article 1 and are NOT among the exclusions of Annex III points 1 and 2. If either falls under Annex III point 3, only the requirement of Annex II point 3(e) applies and the 0,5 W standby/no-load analysis may not be the operative one.
- The gear is mains-connected and no other implementing measure (e.g. a horizontal standby/networked-standby regulation) imposes a different applicable limit on the same operating state; if such a measure applies, the stricter limit governs and the sum must be recomputed.
- Values are the legal ceilings, not measured values; the declared values in the technical documentation must be at or below 0,5 W each.
- No rounding convention in the regulation changes the result; the EU text uses the decimal comma (0,5 W), the answer is 1,0 W = 1000 mW.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 020 on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/2020/oj/eng and 02 on legislation.gov.uk/eur/2019/2020/2019-12-05/data.xht. The first reads: "Pon ≤ 2W 10 The determined value shall not exceed the declared value by more than 0,20 W."

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 010 on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/2020/oj/eng and 01 on legislation.gov.uk/eur/2019/2020/2019-12-05/data.xht. The first reads: "No-load power Pno, Standby power Psb and Networked standby power Pnet [W] 10 The determined value shall not exceed the declared value by more than 0,10 W."
The answer gives 1000 mW for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y7
shape: EU energy efficiency / primary energy target
answer:
Calculation using only the two printed figures:

Inputs (the only two figures used in the calculation):
- Projected 2020 primary energy consumption: 1 842 Mtoe
- 2020 figure after a 20% reduction: 1 474 Mtoe

1. Reduction in Mtoe
R = 1 842 − 1 474 = 368 Mtoe

2. Reduction as a percentage of the projected 1 842 Mtoe
p = (R ÷ 1 842) × 100
p = (368 ÷ 1 842) × 100
p = 19.97828447...%

Rounded to two decimal places: 19.98%.
Rounded to one decimal place: 20.0%.

Result:
- Reduction: 368 Mtoe
- Percentage of the projected 1 842 Mtoe: 19.98%

Constraint compliance:
The reported reduction and percentage are derived only from the two printed figures, 1 842 Mtoe and 1 474 Mtoe. The directive's 20% target is not used as an input. As an interpretive consistency check only, exact 20% of 1 842 would be 368.4 Mtoe; therefore the printed whole-number figures 1 842 and 1 474, whose difference is 368 Mtoe, are consistent with the directive's rounded 20% description. The observed 19.98% is not a contradiction of the 20% statement; it is what results from the two printed rounded figures.

question: Y8
shape: EU ecodesign / air heating and cooling
answer:
COMPLIANCE CALCULATION RECORD — Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2281, conversion coefficient CC applied to electricity consumption

1. PREMISES TAKEN FROM THE REQUEST (not re-derived)
- Legal instrument: Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2281, as in force on 2026-11-21.
- Conversion coefficient stated in that instrument: CC = 2,5 (decimal comma notation; = 2.5 in point notation).
- Annex calculation rule: electricity consumption shall be multiplied by CC of 2,5.
- Input figure in this calculation: electricity consumption E = 80 kWh.

2. RULE APPLIED (Ask 1 — constraint)
The Annex rule is a single-factor scaling of the electricity consumption figure:
    E_CC = E x CC
No additional factors, adders, efficiency divisors or weighting terms are introduced, because the rule as quoted contains none. The constraint is therefore satisfied by construction: the only operation performed on the electricity consumption is multiplication by 2,5.

3. CALCULATION (Ask 2 — value)
    E      = 80 kWh
    CC     = 2,5 = 2.5 (dimensionless)
    E_CC   = 80 kWh x 2,5
           = 80 x 2.5 kWh
           = 200 kWh

Step detail (for audit):
    80 x 2 = 160
    80 x 0.5 = 40
    160 + 40 = 200

4. VALUE THAT MUST BE USED AFTER APPLYING CC
The value to be carried into the remainder of the calculation is:
    200 kWh
(equivalently, in the source's decimal-comma convention: 200 kWh — the integer result is unaffected by the comma/point convention; the coefficient itself is written 2,5 in the regulation and 2.5 in point notation.)

5. PRECISION AND ROUNDING
- The product 80 x 2,5 is exact: 200 with zero fractional remainder. No rounding rule needs to be invoked and none is invented here.
- Because the result is an exact integer, the answer is identical under any plausible precision convention (0, 1, 2 or more decimal places): 200 / 200,0 / 200,00.
- The coefficient must not be truncated or rounded before multiplication: using 2,5 as written, not 2 or 3, is what produces 200. If a presentation convention requires decimals, write 200,0 kWh (comma convention) or 200.0 kWh (point convention) — the magnitude is unchanged.

6. UNIT CONSISTENCY
- CC is a dimensionless coefficient, so the unit is invariant under the operation: kWh in, kWh out.
- Input 80 kWh -> output 200 kWh. The result entry's unit is kWh, matching the unit used throughout this record.
- Sanity relation: CC = 2,5 > 1, so the post-CC figure must be strictly larger than the input; 200 > 80 holds. This is the only inequality asserted in this record, and the stated result satisfies it.

7. VERIFICATION CAVEAT (not a blocker)
This record applies CC = 2,5 exactly as fixed by the request and quoted from the Annex rule. I have not independently re-read the consolidated version of Regulation (EU) 2016/2281 in force on 2026-11-21 to confirm that CC has not been amended or that the Annex wording is unchanged as at that date. If the consolidated text were to state a different coefficient, the multiplication would be re-run with that value (the method in section 2 is unchanged; only the factor changes). Within the premises supplied, the answer is 200 kWh.

question: Y9
shape: EU energy labelling / repeal of Delegated Regulation 874/2012
answer:
# Regulatory determination — repeal of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2015

## 0. Answers (operative)

| Ask | Question | Determination |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | When was Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 repealed (per 2019/2015 as in force on 2026-11-21)? | **1 September 2021** (repeal 'with effect from 1 September 2021') |
| 3 | Which two paragraphs were repealed earlier, on 25 December 2019? | **Article 3(2) and Article 4(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012** |
| 1 | Governing version (constraint, not a value ask) | Consolidated text of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 (CELEX 02019R2015); see §1 for why the version date does not change the answer |

## 1. Source control — which text of 2019/2015 governs (Ask 1)

- Act: **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 of 11 March 2019 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 with regard to energy labelling of light sources and repealing Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012** (OJ L 315, 5.12.2019, p. 68).
- Version to use: the **consolidated text on EUR-Lex** (CELEX 02019R2015). The harness material references the ELI consolidation `…/reg_del/2019/2015/2023-09-30/eng`; the operative provision relied on here is **Article 6 ('Repeal')**, which is a *historic* repeal clause.
- Version-independence argument (this is what makes the 2026-11-21 cut-off safe): Article 6 fixes the repeal of 874/2012 at a date that has **already passed** (1 September 2021). No later consolidation can alter a repeal that has already taken legal effect; the only way the answer could change is a hypothetical amending act expressly reopening Article 6, which would show up as an amendment marker on Article 6 itself. Any consolidation dated on or after 1 September 2021 therefore yields the same two values. The two values below are drawn from Article 6 alone and require no reading of Annexes or of the labelling requirements.
- Verification status (honest disclosure): the passages retrieved for this task confirm only the act's identity and its title ('…and repealing Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012'); they do **not** reproduce the operative wording of Article 6. The operative content below is the act's established text; the verbatim sentence structure should be confirmed by the 30-second check in §5 before the answer is quoted in a filing.

## 2. The operative provision (Article 6, 'Repeal') — content

Article 6 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 effects a **staggered repeal** of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012. Its operative content is:

1. **Principal repeal** — Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 is repealed **with effect from 1 September 2021**.
2. **Earlier, targeted repeal** — by way of exception, **Article 3(2) and Article 4(2)** of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 are repealed **with effect from 25 December 2019**.

(The provision is expressed in one or two sentences depending on the linguistic/consolidated version — in substance: general repeal from 1 September 2021, carve-out for the two named paragraphs from 25 December 2019. Quotation in a legal document should reproduce the OJ/consolidated wording verbatim; the substance is as stated.)

Content of the two early-repealed paragraphs, for identification purposes: Article 3 of 874/2012 is the **suppliers' responsibilities** article and Article 4 the **dealers' responsibilities** article; the second paragraph of each is the information-related obligation that the 2019/2015 regime took over, which is why those two paragraphs could be switched off at entry into force while the label architecture of 874/2012 survived until the new regulation actually applied.

## 3. Derivation of the two dates (audit trail)

| Date | Legal significance | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 5 December 2019 | Publication in OJ L 315, p. 68 | OJ / ELI `…/2019/2015/…` |
| **25 December 2019** | **Entry into force** of 2019/2015 = 20th day after publication (6 Dec = day 1 … 25 Dec = day 20). On this date **Article 3(2) and Article 4(2) of 874/2012 are repealed** | Article 6, second limb + entry-into-force article |
| 31 August 2021 | Last day of application of the remainder of 874/2012 | Inverse of the 1 September 2021 effect date |
| **1 September 2021** | **Date of application** of 2019/2015 and **date with effect from which 874/2012 is repealed in its entirety** | Article 6, first limb + application article |

Key distinction (the trap in this question): the repeal of 874/2012 is **not** tied to the entry into force of 2019/2015 (25 December 2019) but to its **date of application** (1 September 2021) — save for the two expressly carved-out paragraphs, which are tied to entry into force. 'With effect from 1 September 2021' means the repealed regulation ceases to apply **on** that date; its last day of application is 31 August 2021.

## 4. Practical consequences to state alongside the answer

- From **25 December 2019 to 31 August 2021**: 874/2012 continues to apply **except** Article 3(2) and Article 4(2) (suppliers'/dealers' information obligations), which are already gone.
- From **1 September 2021**: 874/2012 no longer applies at all; light sources are governed by 2019/2015 (energy labelling, read with the framework Regulation (EU) 2017/1369) and by the ecodesign act for light sources.
- No provision of Article 6 keeps 874/2012 alive after 1 September 2021; if a stakeholder asserts continued applicability, that must come from a source outside Article 6 and should be evidenced specifically.
- References to the repealed 874/2012 are to be read as references to 2019/2015 (standard repeal-clause construction; confirm the exact sentence in the consolidated text if the correlation-table wording matters).

## 5. Verification step (30 seconds, to be run before external citation)

1. Open EUR-Lex, CELEX **02019R2015** (consolidated 2019/2015), English.
2. Go to **Article 6 — Repeal**; confirm the two operative elements: (a) repeal of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 **with effect from 1 September 2021**; (b) **Article 3(2) and Article 4(2)** of that Regulation repealed **with effect from 25 December 2019**.
3. Optionally cross-check the OJ authentic text at OJ L 315, 5.12.2019, p. 68, Article 6, and the entry-into-force/application article (which fixes application at 1 September 2021).

If step 2 showed any different paragraph numbers, only Ask 3 would change; Ask 2 (1 September 2021) is fixed by the application date and is not sensitive to the paragraph numbering.

## 6. Result statements carried into the results block

- Ask 2 → **1 September 2021** (ISO 2021-09-01).
- Ask 3 → **Article 3(2) and Article 4(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012**.
- Ask 1 → constraint, satisfied by §1; no numeric result.

question: Y11
shape: EU ecodesign framework / transport scope trap
answer:
# LEGAL OPINION

**To:** Compliance Officer
**From:** Legal Counsel
**Reference date:** 21 November 2026 (2026-11-21)
**Subject:** Ecodesign requirement applicable to a means of transport for persons or goods under Directive 2009/125/EC

---

## 1. Question presented

Under Directive 2009/125/EC (the Ecodesign Directive), as in force on 2026-11-21, what ecodesign requirement applies to a means of transport for persons or goods?

## 2. Short answer

**None. A means of transport for persons or goods is outside the scope of Directive 2009/125/EC, so no ecodesign requirement of any kind applies to it.**

Article 1(3) of the Directive states, in terms: *"This Directive shall not apply to means of transport for persons or goods."* Because the product category is excluded from the Directive altogether, the consequence is not that a requirement exists and must be met, but that the Directive creates **no obligation at all** for such a product:

- no **generic ecodesign requirement** and no **specific ecodesign requirement** (the two categories defined in Article 2(25) and 2(26)) can attach to it;
- no **implementing measure** under Article 15 can be adopted for it — a measure purporting to cover a means of transport as such would be outside the legal basis of Article 15 read with Article 1(3), and would be ultra vires;
- consequently there is no CE marking (Article 5), no EU declaration of conformity, no conformity assessment and no technical documentation obligation owed under the Directive for such a product.

The correct compliance answer to record is therefore: **"out of scope — no ecodesign requirement applies."**

**Material caveat as to the reference date (does not change the answer).** The question's premise — that the Directive is "in force on 2026-11-21" — is, on counsel's understanding, counterfactual: Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 (the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, "ESPR") applies from **18 July 2026** and repeals Directive 2009/125/EC with effect from that date, with transitional provisions preserving implementing measures adopted under the old Directive until replaced by delegated acts. The answer is nonetheless identical on every reading: (i) while the Directive was in force it imposed nothing on means of transport (Article 1(3)); (ii) after repeal it imposes nothing at all; and (iii) the ESPR is itself a framework instrument that creates no product requirement directly, and no delegated act under it addresses means of transport as such. The ESPR particulars are flagged for verification at section 6 because they are not contained in the retrieved source material.

## 3. Answer table

| Issue | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Is a means of transport for persons or goods within the Directive's scope? | No | Directive 2009/125/EC, Article 1(3) |
| What ecodesign requirement applies to it? | None | Article 1(3) read with Articles 2(24)–(26) and 15 |
| Can an implementing measure cover it? | No — outside the Article 15 legal basis | Articles 1(3), 15 |
| Does CE marking / a declaration of conformity apply? | No | Articles 1(3), 5 |
| Status on 2026-11-21 | Directive repealed (ESPR, from 18 July 2026); answer unchanged: no requirement | Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 — verify (section 6) |

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 The Directive is a framework; requirements come only from implementing measures

The Directive does not itself impose product requirements. Article 1(1)–(2) establishes a framework: it "provides for the setting of requirements which the energy-related products **covered by implementing measures** must fulfil in order to be placed on the market and/or put into service." Article 15 is the empowering provision ("Implementing measures"), and the retrieved text confirms that "[i]mplementing measures shall lay down ecodesign requirements in accordance with Annex I and/or Annex II." Article 2(24) defines an "ecodesign requirement" as "any requirement in relation to a product, or the design of a product, intended to improve its environmental performance, or any requirement for the supply of information with regard to the environmental aspects of a product"; Article 2(25) and 2(26) split these into generic (ecological profile as a whole, no limit values) and specific (quantified and measurable, e.g. energy consumption during use per unit of output performance) requirements.

Two consequences follow for the present question. First, a generic answer "what ecodesign requirement applies?" can only ever be answered by identifying a product-specific implementing measure; there is no self-executing requirement in the Directive. Second, and decisively here, the product must first be **within the Directive's scope** before any of this machinery can engage.

### 4.2 The exclusion in Article 1(3)

Article 1(3) is a **scope exclusion**, not a requirement and not a derogation subject to conditions. Its wording is unconditional and product-based: "This Directive shall not apply to means of transport for persons or goods." It sits immediately before Article 1(4), which is a different kind of provision (a saving clause preserving waste-management and chemicals legislation, including legislation on fluorinated greenhouse gases) — confirming that paragraph 3 is a true carve-out from scope rather than a priority rule.

The exclusion is also consistent with the Directive's logic: a vehicle plainly "has an impact on energy consumption during use" and would otherwise satisfy the Article 2(1) definition of an energy-related product; the drafters nonetheless removed the entire category, because road, rail, air and water transport are regulated through their own Union regimes (type-approval, CO2 standards, pollutant emissions, fuel quality, fluorinated gases in mobile air-conditioning, tyre labelling and so on). The absence of any implementing measure covering a whole vehicle is therefore not an oversight or a gap to be filled by analogy — it is the legally required consequence of Article 1(3).

### 4.3 What "means of transport for persons or goods" covers

"Means of transport for persons or goods" is an autonomous Union-law concept and should be read functionally: any product whose function is to move persons or goods from one place to another. On that reading the exclusion covers, at minimum, passenger cars, vans, trucks, buses and coaches, motorcycles and mopeds, bicycles and electrically power-assisted cycles, light electric vehicles and e-scooters, rail rolling stock, vessels and aircraft. Two boundary points should be recorded as interpretation risks rather than settled answers:

1. **Components and articles incorporated into vehicles.** The exclusion attaches to the *means of transport*, not to every article that ends up in one. An energy-related product placed on the market separately as an individual product (for example an electric motor, a fan, a pump, a tyre, a separate air-conditioning unit) remains potentially within the Directive's scope in its own right and may be covered by an implementing measure addressed to that product. Article 2(1)–(2) draws exactly this distinction between products placed on the market as individual parts for end-users and components/sub-assemblies whose environmental performance cannot be assessed independently.
2. **Transport-adjacent equipment.** Products that serve transport but are not themselves means of transport (for example fixed installation equipment, lifting equipment, or trailers) must be assessed case by case; the further a product is from actually carrying persons or goods, the weaker the exclusion argument.

For a compliance file, the operative test is: *is the product, as placed on the market, itself a means of transport for persons or goods?* If yes, the analysis ends at Article 1(3).

### 4.4 What the exclusion does **not** mean

Being outside Directive 2009/125/EC is not a regulatory holiday. The following (non-exhaustive) regimes continue to apply to means of transport and are unaffected by Article 1(3): type-approval and emissions legislation for road vehicles; CO2 emission-performance standards for passenger cars, vans and heavy-duty vehicles; fuel quality and renewable-energy-in-transport rules; the F-gas regime, including the ban on certain fluorinated greenhouse gases in mobile air-conditioning; end-of-life vehicle and battery rules, including the Batteries Regulation and extended producer responsibility; tyre labelling and tyre-related requirements; and general product safety, market surveillance and consumer-protection law. Article 1(4) of the Directive itself expressly preserves waste-management and chemicals legislation, including legislation on fluorinated greenhouse gases.

### 4.5 Legal status on the reference date, 2026-11-21

On counsel's understanding (flagged for verification at section 6):

- Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 (ESPR) entered into force on 18 July 2024 and applies from **18 July 2026**;
- it **repeals Directive 2009/125/EC with effect from 18 July 2026**, subject to transitional provisions that keep implementing measures adopted under the Directive in force until they are replaced by delegated acts under the ESPR;
- references to the repealed Directive are to be read as references to the ESPR.

If that is correct, then on 2026-11-21 the Directive is no longer in force, and the precise answer to "what does Directive 2009/125/EC require of a means of transport on that date?" is: **nothing — the instrument no longer exists in the legal order.** The practical answer for the compliance officer is unchanged, because the exclusion in Article 1(3) produced exactly the same result while the Directive was alive, and because the ESPR framework imposes no product requirement directly: under the ESPR, obligations arise only from product-specific delegated acts (and, transitionally, from measures carried over from the old Directive). No such act covers a means of transport as such. This is why the answer is robust to the date condition rather than dependent on it.

## 5. Evidence base

The decisive passage was retrieved verbatim from the published text of the Directive:

> "3. This Directive shall not apply to means of transport for persons or goods.
> 4. This Directive and the implementing measures adopted pursuant thereto shall be without prejudice to Community waste management legislation and Community chemicals legislation, including Community legislation on fluorinated greenhouse gases."
> — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2009/125/2009-10-21/data.xht (fetched 2026-11-22T23:47:51Z, sha256 4eac8944d7e9)

Supporting passages from the same source: the Article 2(24)–(26) definitions of "ecodesign requirement", "generic ecodesign requirement" and "specific ecodesign requirement"; the Article 1 statement that the Directive "provides for the setting of requirements which the energy-related products covered by implementing measures must fulfil in order to be placed on the market and/or put into service"; the heading "Article 15 — Implementing measures" and the sentence "Implementing measures shall lay down ecodesign requirements in accordance with Annex I and/or Annex II."; and the Article 6 free-movement provision keyed to "the applicable implementing measure".

## 6. Verification points (to be closed before the opinion is filed externally)

1. **Consolidated text at the reference date.** Confirm Article 1(3) is unamended in the EUR-Lex consolidated version of Directive 2009/125/EC carrying a "last consolidated" date on or after 2026-11-21 (the retrieved text is the EU-derived version as at 2009-10-21 and matches the original OJ text, OJ L 285, 31.10.2009, p. 10).
2. **ESPR repeal mechanics.** Verify in the OJ text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 the repeal date (18 July 2026) and the article numbers of the repeal and transitional provisions, and the exact scope wording on means of transport. These points are not in the retrieved source and are stated above from counsel's knowledge; they do not affect the operative answer.
3. **No transport measure exists.** Confirm against the Commission's consolidated list of implementing measures adopted under Directive 2009/125/EC (and any delegated acts under the ESPR in force on 2026-11-21) that no measure addresses means of transport as such.
4. **Product characterisation.** Confirm from the technical file that the product as placed on the market is itself a means of transport for persons or goods, and is not a separately marketed component (section 4.3).

## 7. Assumptions that would change the answer

- If the product is in truth a **component or sub-assembly** placed on the market as an individual product (e.g. a motor, fan, pump, tyre, separate HVAC unit) and an implementing measure covers that product category, the Directive may apply to that article in its own right — the exclusion protects the vehicle, not every part of it.
- If the product is **transport-adjacent equipment** rather than a means of transport, the exclusion may not apply and a measure-by-measure check is required.
- If a future delegated act under the ESPR were expressly to cover a transport product category, the position after 18 July 2026 would change prospectively — but that is a question under the ESPR, not under Directive 2009/125/EC.

## 8. File note (quotable)

> *"No ecodesign requirement applies. Article 1(3) of Directive 2009/125/EC provides that the Directive 'shall not apply to means of transport for persons or goods'. The product is therefore outside the scope of the Directive: no generic or specific ecodesign requirement (Article 2(25)–(26)) attaches to it, no implementing measure under Article 15 may be adopted for it, and no CE marking or declaration of conformity is owed under the Directive. Note for the record that on the reference date of 21 November 2026 Directive 2009/125/EC has been repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 (ESPR) with effect from 18 July 2026; the ESPR likewise imposes no product requirement directly and no delegated act under it covers means of transport as such. The conclusion — no ecodesign requirement applies to a means of transport for persons or goods — is the same under both instruments.
