Separate transport-specific Union legislation (type-approval, CO2 standards, emissions, F-gas, end-of-life vehicle and battery rules, tyre labelling) continues to apply and should be assessed independently."*

question: Y12
shape: EU electric motors / medium voltage trap
answer:
ANSWER (bottom line)

Under Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/1781, as in force on 2026-11-21, NO minimum energy-efficiency class is set for electric motors with a rated voltage above 1 000 V. Such motors fall outside the product scope of the Regulation entirely. The correct answer to 'what minimum energy-efficiency class is set?' is therefore: none — the Regulation does not set one, because it does not apply to those motors at all. It is not IE1, IE2, IE3 or IE4; the question of an IE class simply does not arise.

This is a scope answer, not an exemption answer, and the distinction matters for compliance practice (see section 4).


1. THE CONTROLLING TEXT

Article 2(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 defines the motor scope. A motor is in scope only if it is an induction electric motor without brushes, commutators, slip rings or electrical connections to the rotor, rated for 50 Hz, 60 Hz or 50/60 Hz sinusoidal voltage, and:

  (i)   has two, four, six or eight poles; AND
  (ii)  has a rated voltage U_N above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V; AND
  (iii) has a rated power output P_N from 0,12 kW up to and including 1 000 kW; AND
  (iv)  is rated on the basis of continuous duty operation; AND
  (v)   is rated for direct on-line operation.

The five conditions are cumulative ('that: (i) ... (ii) ...'). Condition (ii) is a hard ceiling at 1 000 V. A motor whose rated voltage U_N exceeds 1 000 V fails condition (ii) and is not a product to which the Regulation applies.

Article 1 confirms the framing: the Regulation 'establishes ecodesign requirements for the placing on the market or the putting into service of electric motors and variable speed drives' — i.e. only for the products defined in Article 2.

The efficiency obligations themselves live in Annex I, section 1, and are drafted as obligations on motors that are already in scope:
  - from 1 July 2021: three-phase motors of 0,75 kW to 1 000 kW (2, 4, 6, 8 poles), other than Ex eb increased-safety motors, must reach at least IE3 (Annex I, Table 2); three-phase motors of 0,12 kW to below 0,75 kW must reach at least IE2 (Annex I, Table 1);
  - from 1 July 2023: Ex eb increased-safety motors of 0,12 kW to 1 000 kW and single-phase motors from 0,12 kW must reach at least IE2 (Annex I, Table 1).

Every one of those thresholds is expressed in kW, poles and IE level — none of them extends, widens or overrides the 1 000 V voltage ceiling in Article 2(1)(a)(ii). The Annex cannot pull into scope a motor that Article 2 has left out; a requirement in Annex I applies only to products within the Article 2 scope. So there is no route by which a >1 000 V motor acquires an IE obligation.


2. THE REGULATION'S OWN CORROBORATION

Article 9 (Review) requires the Commission to review the Regulation and, in particular, to address the appropriateness of, at point (4):

  'setting minimum energy efficiency requirements for motors with a rated voltage above 1000 V'

This is decisive internal evidence. The drafter lists requirements above 1 000 V as something that might be considered in the future, which necessarily means no such requirement exists in the instrument as adopted. If a minimum class had been set for >1 000 V motors, Article 9(4) could not be drafted that way. The same Article lists other forward-looking items (permanent-magnet motors, compact drives, stricter levels, review of the Article 2(2) and 2(3) exemptions) on the same footing — all things not currently regulated.


3. 'AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21' — VERSION CHECK

(a) The scope wording. The Article 2(1)(a)(ii) ceiling of 'above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V' appears unchanged in the adopted OJ text and in the consolidated version of the Regulation (consolidation dated 2023-01-24). No amendment, corrigendum or delegated/implementing act in the material examined alters the voltage ceiling or extends scope to >1 000 V motors.

(b) The review has not produced a requirement. Article 9 set 14 November 2023 as the deadline for presenting the review, including 'if appropriate, a draft revision proposal'. A review clause is a procedural obligation on the Commission; it does not itself impose any requirement on manufacturers, and it does not amend Article 2. Even if the review has been completed and a revision proposed, a proposal is not law. The question is expressly about Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 as in force on 2026-11-21, and in that instrument the voltage ceiling stands.

(c) Residual-risk caveat, stated honestly. It is conceivable that a separate, later instrument (for example a replacement ecodesign regulation for motors and variable speed drives adopted under Directive 2009/125/EC) could be in force by 2026-11-21 and could change the voltage scope. That would be a different legal instrument and would not change what Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 itself provides; the question as put is answered by 2019/1781. A supplier doing a live conformity assessment should nevertheless run the check in section 6 before relying on this answer for a 2026 placement.


4. WHAT 'OUT OF SCOPE' MEANS IN PRACTICE — AND THE TRAP TO AVOID

Do not describe a >1 000 V motor as an 'exempted motor'. The Regulation has two different mechanisms and they have different consequences:

  - Article 2(1) — scope. Defines what a 'motor' is for the purposes of the Regulation. A >1 000 V machine is not a product covered by the Regulation at all.
  - Article 2(2) — exemptions. Applies to motors that ARE within Article 2(1) but are relieved of part of Annex I. Examples listed: motors completely integrated into a product and not testable independently; compact drives whose performance cannot be tested independently; motors with an integrated brake forming part of the inner construction; motors specified exclusively for altitudes above 4 000 m, ambient air above 60 °C, maximum operating temperature above 400 °C, ambient below -30 °C, or water coolant inlet below 0 °C or above 32 °C; motors designed to operate wholly immersed in a liquid; motors qualified for nuclear installation safety; explosion-protected motors certified for mining; motors in cordless/battery-operated equipment; hand-held and hand-guided mobile equipment motors; motors with mechanical commutators; TENV motors; multi-speed motors; EV traction motors; and pre-2029 service substitutes for motors integrated in products placed on the market before 1 July 2022.

Consequences of the scope exclusion (Article 2(1)(a)(ii)) for a >1 000 V motor:
  - no minimum IE class and no efficiency obligation under this Regulation;
  - no obligation under this Regulation to draw up the technical documentation, declare conformity, affix CE marking for ecodesign, or supply the Annex I section 2 product information (efficiency at 50/75/100 % load, etc.);
  - no verification tolerances, no market-surveillance exposure under this Regulation.

Consequences that remain: the machine is still subject to whatever other law applies to it — e.g. machinery safety law, EMC, and electrical safety rules applicable above 1 000 V AC (the Low Voltage Directive 2014/35/EU is itself limited to 50-1 000 V AC, so high-voltage machines are governed by other safety regimes, not by the LVD). Those are separate regimes; none of them imposes an IE class. Note also that IEC 60034-30-1, the efficiency classification standard the Regulation's IE levels are built on, is itself limited to machines up to 1 000 V, which is consistent with there being no IE classification to assign above that voltage.


5. BOUNDARY CASES — HOW TO CLASSIFY AT THE EDGE

  - Rated voltage exactly 1 000 V: IN scope. The wording is 'up to and including 1 000 V'.
  - Rated voltage 1 001 V or higher (e.g. 3 kV, 6 kV, 6,6 kV, 10 kV, 11 kV): OUT of scope. No IE class.
  - Dual/range-rated machine (e.g. nameplate 690/1 000 V, or 500-1 100 V): the scope test is applied to the rated voltage(s) for which the motor is placed on the market. A machine that can be placed on the market rated above 1 000 V should not be treated as in scope on the strength of a lower rating; treat the >1 000 V configuration as outside scope and document the reasoning. This is a boundary judgement, not a textually resolved point — record it in the technical file.
  - Do not confuse the two 1 000s. Article 2(1)(a)(ii) caps VOLTAGE at 1 000 V; Article 2(1)(a)(iii) caps POWER OUTPUT at 1 000 kW. A 900 kW, 6 kV motor fails the voltage condition and is out of scope despite being under 1 000 kW. A 1 500 kW, 690 V motor fails the power condition and is out of scope despite being under 1 000 V. Either failure is sufficient.
  - Wound-rotor/slip-ring machines above 1 000 V are out of scope twice over (slip rings, and voltage).
  - Legacy confusion with Regulation (EC) No 640/2009: that Regulation, repealed by 2019/1781, also covered only motors up to 1 000 V. There is no earlier regime under which a >1 000 V motor carried an IE obligation, so no transitional reading produces a different answer.


6. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (for a live determination on or before 2026-11-21)

Step 1 — Read the nameplate / technical file. Record U_N, P_N, number of poles, duty, supply frequency, starting method (DOL vs inverter-only), and whether the machine is an induction motor without brushes, commutators, slip rings or rotor electrical connections.
Step 2 — Apply Article 2(1)(a) cumulatively. If U_N > 1 000 V, stop: the product is outside scope, no IE class, no obligations under this Regulation. Record 'outside scope of Regulation (EU) 2019/1781, Article 2(1)(a)(ii)' in the technical file.
Step 3 — If U_N is at or below 1 000 V, continue: check 50-1 000 V, 0,12-1 000 kW, 2/4/6/8 poles, continuous duty, DOL rating. If all pass, the motor is in scope.
Step 4 — For an in-scope motor, check Article 2(2)(a)-(o) exemptions; if one applies, note which and which Annex I provisions are disapplied.
Step 5 — For an in-scope, non-exempt motor, read the applicable Annex I section 1 row by date: from 1 July 2021, IE3 for 0,75-1 000 kW three-phase non-Ex-eb, IE2 for 0,12-<0,75 kW; from 1 July 2023, IE2 for Ex eb increased-safety motors 0,12-1 000 kW and for single-phase motors from 0,12 kW. Compare the measured efficiency against Table 1 or Table 2 as applicable.
Step 6 — Version control for the 2026-11-21 date: check the EUR-Lex 'all consolidated versions' list for Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 and the OJ L series for any amending act adopted between 1 December 2019 and 21 November 2026; confirm Article 2(1)(a)(ii) still reads 'above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V'. Also check whether any separate, later ecodesign instrument for motors has entered into force by that date, and whether it (not 2019/1781) governs the product.


7. ERROR MODES THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST

  - Answering 'IE3' or 'IE2' by pattern-matching the Annex I timetable without applying the Article 2 scope filter. The timetable applies only to in-scope motors.
  - Answering 'IE4' — no IE4 minimum is set anywhere in this Regulation for any motor.
  - Reading Article 9(4) as if it imposed a requirement above 1 000 V. It is a review clause; it is evidence that no such requirement exists.
  - Treating the >1 000 V machine as 'exempt under Article 2(2)'. Wrong mechanism; Article 2(2) presupposes an in-scope motor.
  - Conflating the 1 000 V voltage ceiling with the 1 000 kW power ceiling.
  - Assuming the 14 November 2023 review deadline created law. It did not.

BOTTOM LINE, RESTATED FOR THE RECORD: Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 sets no minimum energy-efficiency class for electric motors with a rated voltage above 1 000 V, because Article 2(1)(a)(ii) limits the product scope to motors rated above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V. The correct answer is: no IE class applies — such motors are outside the scope of the Regulation.

question: Y14

answer:
# Portable-battery classification: Directive 2006/66/EC vs. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542

Purpose: supply the two definitions in citable form so the classification procedure can be red-lined, with the exact conditions, the exact threshold and the exact exclusions, plus a paste-ready decision procedure and worked boundary cases.

---

## 0. Sources used

| Ref | Text | Version / locator | Provision relied on |
|---|---|---|---|
| **D** | Directive 2006/66/EC on batteries and accumulators and waste batteries and accumulators (OJ L 266, 26.9.2006, p. 1), as amended by Directive 2013/56/EU | Consolidated text, EUR-Lex ELI `https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/66/2018-07-04`; corroborated by `https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2006/66/body?view=plain` and the OJ-derived PDF at `http://publications.europa.eu/resource/cellar/4e67c14e-7e38-4e93-9321-105c2fa05a07.0006.03/DOC_2` | Art. 3(1), 3(3), 3(4), 3(5), 3(6); the recital giving examples of portable batteries and accumulators |
| **R** | Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 concerning batteries and waste batteries, amending Directive 2008/98/EC and Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and repealing Directive 2006/66/EC (OJ L 191, 28.7.2023, p. 1) | Consolidated text `02023R1542 — EN — 28.07.2023 — 000.005` (`https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02023R1542-20230728`) and the version at `https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1542/2026-08-13/eng`; OJ PDF `https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32023R1542` | Art. 1 (scope); Art. 3(1)(1), (9), (10), (11), (12), (13), (14); recital (15) (and recital (14) on DIY kits) |

The definition of 'portable battery' in Art. 3(1)(9) R is worded identically in the 28.07.2023 consolidated text and in the 2026-08-13 consolidated text (which records amendments M1 2024/1781, M2 2025/1561, M3 2026/1738 and corrigenda C1–C4); none of those amendments or corrigenda touches point (9) as fetched. Quote Art. 3(1)(9) as it stands in the consolidated text.

---

## 1. Directive 2006/66/EC — the three conditions (answer to ask 2)

### 1.1 Verbatim definition — Article 3(3)

> "(3) 'portable battery or accumulator' means any battery, button cell, battery pack or accumulator that:
> (a) is sealed; and
> (b) can be hand-carried; and
> (c) is neither an industrial battery or accumulator nor an automotive battery or accumulator;"

*(Directive 2006/66/EC, Art. 3(3); identical wording in the consolidated EUR-Lex text, the legislation.gov.uk text and the OJ-derived PDF.)*

### 1.2 The three conditions

All three are joined by "and" — they are **cumulative**, and each must be satisfied before the object is a portable battery or accumulator.

| # | Condition | Operative wording | What the auditor must test / evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Sealed** | "is sealed" | The unit is closed and not intended to be opened or refilled by the end-user. Applies to the battery, button cell, battery pack or accumulator as placed on the market. |
| **2** | **Can be hand-carried** | "can be hand-carried" | A **functional/ergonomic** test, not a numeric one. The Directive's examples recital glosses it as "an average person could carry by hand without difficulty". There is **no kilogram figure** anywhere in the Directive. Do not substitute 5 kg. |
| **3** | **Not industrial and not automotive** | "is neither an industrial battery or accumulator nor an automotive battery or accumulator" | Two negative category tests, resolved against Art. 3(5) and Art. 3(6) (below). |

**No weight limit exists in Directive 2006/66/EC.** This is the single most common defect in procedures that quote this definition: a 5 kg line is imported from the 2023 Regulation and mis-attributed to the Directive. Under the Directive a sealed, hand-carryable 7 kg unit can still be a portable battery or accumulator if it is neither industrial nor automotive.

### 1.3 The forms covered

The definition expressly catches "any battery, **button cell**, **battery pack** or accumulator". Button cells are therefore portable batteries under the Directive by inclusion, and Art. 3(4) defines them as follows:

> "(4) 'button cell' means any small round portable battery or accumulator whose diameter is greater than its height and which is used for special purposes such as hearing aids, watches, small portable equipment and back-up power;"

### 1.4 The two carve-out categories (condition 3)

> "(5) 'automotive battery or accumulator' means any battery or accumulator used for automotive starter, lighting or ignition power;"

> "(6) 'industrial battery or accumulator' means any battery or accumulator designed for exclusively industrial or professional uses or used in any type of electric vehicle;"

Two points matter for the red-line:

- The Directive's industrial test is **"designed for exclusively industrial or professional uses"** — the adverb *exclusively* is part of the text. A battery intended for professional use but not *exclusively* so is not automatically industrial, and can therefore remain portable if conditions 1 and 2 are met.
- Under the Directive there is **no separate EV category**: a battery "used in any type of electric vehicle" is swept into *industrial* by Art. 3(6), and is thus excluded from portable via condition 3(c).

### 1.5 The examples recital (interpretive aid for condition 2)

> "Examples of portable batteries and accumulators, which are all-sealed batteries and accumulators that an average person could carry by hand without difficulty and that are neither automotive batteries or accumulators nor industrial batteries or accumulators, include single cell batteries (such as AA and AAA batteries) and batteries and accumulators used by consumers or professionals in mobile telephones, portable computers, cordless power tools, toys and household appliances such as electric toothbrushes, razors and hand-held vacuum cleaners (including similar equipment used in schools, shops, restaurants, airports, offices or hospitals) and any battery or accumulator that consumers may use for normal household applications."

This recital confirms (i) that "hand-carried" is measured against an average person and (ii) that *professional* use of a hand-held tool does not by itself make the battery industrial. Cite it by its text; confirm its recital number against the OJ before it is printed in the procedure (see §7).

### 1.6 For completeness — the parent term, Article 3(1)

> "(1) 'battery' or 'accumulator' means any source of electrical energy generated by direct conversion of chemical energy and consisting of one or more primary battery cells (non-rechargeable) or consisting of one or more secondary battery cells (rechargeable);"

---

## 2. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 — weight limit and exclusions (answers to asks 3 and 4)

### 2.1 Verbatim definition — Article 3(1)(9)

> "(9) 'portable battery' means a battery that is sealed, weighs 5 kg or less, is not designed specifically for industrial use and is neither an electric vehicle battery, an LMT battery, nor an SLI battery;"

*(Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 3(1)(9).)*

### 2.2 Element-by-element breakdown

| # | Element | Operative wording | Type | Test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sealed | "is sealed" | Positive criterion | As under the Directive: closed, not intended to be opened by the end-user. |
| 2 | **Weight limit** | **"weighs 5 kg or less"** | Positive criterion, numeric | **≤ 5.00 kg.** The threshold is **inclusive**: a battery weighing exactly 5 kg is a portable battery. 5.01 kg is not. The 5 kg figure replaces the Directive's "can be hand-carried" test. |
| 3 | **Design exclusion** | "is not designed specifically for industrial use" | Design exclusion | Turns on the **design intent** of the battery, not solely on its actual deployment. "Specifically" qualifies the design purpose. |
| 4a | **Category exclusion — EV** | "neither an electric vehicle battery" | Category exclusion | See Art. 3(1)(12) below. |
| 4b | **Category exclusion — LMT** | "an LMT battery" | Category exclusion | See Art. 3(1)(11) below. |
| 4c | **Category exclusion — SLI** | "nor an SLI battery" | Category exclusion | See Art. 3(1)(13) below. |

### 2.3 The excluded categories, verbatim

> "(11) 'light means of transport battery' or 'LMT battery' means a battery that is sealed, weighs 25 kg or less and is specifically designed to provide electric power for the traction of wheeled vehicles that can be powered by an electric motor alone or by a combination of motor and human power, including type-approved vehicles of category L within the meaning of Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and that is not an electric vehicle battery;"

> "(12) 'electric vehicle battery' means a battery that is specifically designed to provide electric power for traction in hybrid or electric vehicles of category L as provided for in Regulation (EU) No 168/2013, that weighs more than 25 kg, or a battery that is specifically designed to provide electric power for traction in hybrid or electric vehicles of categories M, N or O as provided for in Regulation (EU) 2018/858;"

> "(13) 'starting, lighting and ignition battery' or 'SLI battery' means a battery that is specifically designed to supply electric power for starting, lighting, or ignition and that can also be used for auxiliary or backup purposes in vehicles, other means of transport or machinery;"

> "(14) 'industrial battery' means a battery that is specifically designed for industrial uses, intended for industrial uses after having been subject to preparation for repurposing or repurposing, or any other battery that weighs more than 5 kg and that is neither an electric vehicle battery, an LMT battery, nor an SLI battery;"

Point (14) is the **residual clause** and it closes the classification system: any battery above 5 kg that is not an EV, LMT or SLI battery **is** an industrial battery. The 5 kg line therefore operates in both directions — at or below 5 kg the battery may be portable; above 5 kg it cannot be portable and defaults to industrial.

### 2.4 The sub-category (do not confuse it with the classification test)

> "(10) 'portable battery of general use' means a portable battery, whether or not rechargeable, that is specifically designed to be interoperable and that has one of the following common formats 4,5 Volts (3R12), button cell, D, C, AA, AAA, AAAA, A23, 9 Volts (PP3);"

"Portable battery of general use" is a **subset** of portable battery (it triggers separate obligations). It is not an alternative route into the portable category, and a battery that is not in one of the listed formats is still a portable battery if Art. 3(1)(9) is met.

### 2.5 Recital (15) — the stated classification logic

> "(15) Within the broad scope of this Regulation, it is appropriate to distinguish between different categories of batteries in accordance with their design and use, independently of their battery chemistry. The classification into portable batteries, on the one hand, and industrial batteries and automotive batteries on the other hand under Directive 2006/66/EC should be further developed to better reflect new developments in the use of batteries. Batteries that are used for traction in electric vehicles and which, under Directive 2006/66/EC, fall under the category of industrial batteries, constitute a large and growing part of the market due to the quick growth of electric road ... [Batteries used for traction in wheeled vehicles are classified as light] means of transport batteries (LMT batteries). Batteries used for traction in other transport vehicles including rail, waterborne and aviation transport or off-road machinery, continue to fall under the category of industrial batteries under this Regulation. The industrial battery category encompasses a broad group of batteries, intended to be used for industrial activities, communication infrastructure, agricultural activities, or generation and distribution of electric energy. Batteries which are given industrial uses after being subject to preparation for repurposing or repurposing, even though they were initially designed for a different use, should be considered to be industrial batteries under this Regulation. In addition to this non exhaustive list of examples, any battery that weighs more than 5 kg that does not fall under any other categories under this Regulation should be considered to be an industrial battery. Batteries used for energy storage in private or domestic environments, should be considered to be industrial batteries for the purposes of this Regulation."

Three operative consequences for the procedure:

1. Classification is by **design and use**, not by chemistry.
2. **>5 kg residual = industrial** (confirms Art. 3(1)(14)).
3. **Domestic/private energy-storage batteries are industrial** — a small home storage unit of, say, 4 kg is therefore *not* a portable battery, notwithstanding that it is sealed and under 5 kg. This is the sharpest divergence from the Directive's outcome for the same product.

Also note recital (14): batteries supplied as a "Do It Yourself" kit that the end-user assembles with commonly available tools are batteries for the purposes of the Regulation; the kit placer is the economic operator.

### 2.6 Scope confirmation — Article 1

> "This Regulation applies to all categories of batteries, namely portable batteries, starting, lighting and ignition batteries (SLI batteries), light means of transport batteries (LMT batteries), electric vehicle batteries and industrial batteries, regardless of their shape, volume, weight, design, material composition, chemistry, use or purpose."

The five categories are exhaustive; every battery placed on the market must be assigned to one of them.

---

## 3. Side-by-side — what changed and what the procedure must reflect

| Feature | Directive 2006/66/EC, Art. 3(3) | Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 3(1)(9) | Action for the procedure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Defined term | "portable battery **or accumulator**" | "portable **battery**" only; "accumulator" is not a defined term in the Regulation | Stop writing "battery or accumulator" when applying the Regulation |
| Size criterion | "can be hand-carried" (functional, no figure) | "weighs 5 kg or less" (numeric, inclusive) | Replace the hand-carried test with a mass test + weighing record; do **not** apply 5 kg to legacy Directive assessments |
| Industrial carve-out | "neither an industrial battery or accumulator …" where industrial = "designed for **exclusively** industrial or professional uses or used in any type of electric vehicle" | "**not designed specifically for industrial use**" (separate design exclusion) | Re-word; the Directive's "exclusively … professional" formula has no equivalent in the Regulation |
| Automotive carve-out | "nor an automotive battery or accumulator" (starter, lighting, ignition) | "nor an **SLI battery**" — starter, lighting or ignition, **and** may also be used for auxiliary or backup purposes in vehicles, other means of transport or machinery | Re-word; the Regulation's SLI is drafted more widely |
| EV batteries | No separate category — absorbed into *industrial* via "used in any type of electric vehicle" | Separate category, Art. 3(1)(12) | Add explicit EV test |
| LMT batteries | No such category | Separate category, Art. 3(1)(11): sealed, ≤ 25 kg, traction of wheeled vehicles (incl. L-category), not an EV battery | Add explicit LMT test — this now removes small e-bike/e-scooter batteries from the portable class |
| Residual category | None stated | Art. 3(1)(14): any battery >5 kg that is not EV/LMT/SLI is industrial | Add residual rule |
| Domestic storage | No rule; typically fell to portable if sealed and hand-carryable | Industrial (recital 15) | Add explicit rule |
| Legal effect | Directive — implemented nationally; repealed by the Regulation | Regulation — directly applicable; repeals Directive 2006/66/EC with effect from 18 February 2024 | Update the legal basis cited in the procedure (see §7 on transitional provisions) |

---

## 4. Paste-ready decision procedure

**Step 0 — Choose the governing instrument.** For any battery placed on the market on or after 18 February 2024 (the date from which Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 applies and Directive 2006/66/EC is repealed), apply Steps 1–5. Use the Directive test in Step 6 only for legacy/historical records relating to batteries placed on the market before that date, or where a national transitional rule expressly refers to the Directive. Never mix the two tests in one assessment.

**Step 1 — Is it a battery?** Apply Art. 3(1)(1) R. If not, stop — the Regulation does not apply.

**Step 2 — Sealed?** Art. 3(1)(9) R, first element. If not sealed → not portable. Go to Step 5.

**Step 3 — Mass.** Weigh the battery as placed on the market and record the mass to two decimal places in kilograms.
- **≤ 5.00 kg** → continue to Step 4.
- **> 5.00 kg** → **not portable**. If it is not an EV battery, an LMT battery or an SLI battery, classify as **industrial** under Art. 3(1)(14). Go to Step 5.

**Step 4 — Apply the one design exclusion and the three category exclusions.** If **any** of the following is true, the battery is **not portable**; assign the category shown:
- **Designed specifically for industrial use** → industrial (Art. 3(1)(14)).
- **Electric vehicle battery** — specifically designed to provide traction power for hybrid/electric vehicles of category L and weighing more than 25 kg, or specifically designed to provide traction power for hybrid/electric vehicles of categories M, N or O → EV battery (Art. 3(1)(12)).
- **LMT battery** — sealed, ≤ 25 kg, specifically designed to provide traction power for wheeled vehicles powered by an electric motor alone or by motor + human power, including L-category type-approved vehicles, and not an EV battery → LMT battery (Art. 3(1)(11)).
- **SLI battery** — specifically designed to supply power for starting, lighting or ignition, and capable of auxiliary or backup use in vehicles, other means of transport or machinery → SLI battery (Art. 3(1)(13)).

Additional rule from recital (15): a battery used for energy storage in private or domestic environments is an **industrial** battery.

**Step 5 — Record the outcome.** If Step 2 = sealed, Step 3 = ≤ 5.00 kg and Step 4 produced no exclusion, the battery is a **portable battery** (Art. 3(1)(9)). Record whether it also meets Art. 3(1)(10) (portable battery of general use). Record the evidence for each element: sealing (construction/technical file), mass (weighing record with date and instrument), design intent (manufacturer's intended use, technical documentation, marketing), and end-use.

**Step 6 — Legacy branch (Directive).** All three of the following must hold: (a) sealed; (b) can be hand-carried by an average person without difficulty; (c) neither an industrial battery or accumulator (designed for exclusively industrial or professional uses, or used in any type of electric vehicle) nor an automotive battery or accumulator (used for automotive starter, lighting or ignition power). No mass threshold applies in this branch.

---

## 5. Worked boundary cases

| Case | Mass | Governing test | Outcome | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AA alkaline cell | ~0.025 kg | R Art. 3(1)(9) | Portable; also portable battery of general use, Art. 3(1)(10) | Sealed, ≤ 5 kg, no exclusion |
| Laptop battery pack | ~0.3 kg | R Art. 3(1)(9) | Portable | Sealed, ≤ 5 kg, not industrial-designed, not EV/LMT/SLI |
| Cordless drill battery pack used by consumers and professionals | ~0.5 kg | R Art. 3(1)(9) | Portable, unless specifically designed for industrial use | Art. 3(1)(9) does not use the Directive's "exclusively industrial or professional" formula |
| Battery **exactly 5.00 kg** | 5.00 kg | R Art. 3(1)(9) | **Portable** | "weighs 5 kg or less" is inclusive |
| Battery **5.10 kg**, not EV/LMT/SLI, not designed for industrial use | 5.10 kg | R Art. 3(1)(9) + 3(1)(14) | **Industrial** | Exceeds 5 kg; residual clause applies |
| Pedelec / e-bike traction battery | 3 kg | R Art. 3(1)(11) | **LMT battery — not portable** | Sealed, ≤ 25 kg, traction of a wheeled vehicle powered by motor + human power. Note: under the Directive the same product would have been assessed against "used in any type of electric vehicle" (industrial) — different route, and the Directive's term "electric vehicle" is undefined |
| Larger pedelec battery | 8 kg | R Art. 3(1)(11) | **LMT battery — not portable** | Still ≤ 25 kg; the 5 kg line is irrelevant once the LMT test is met |
| L-category traction battery | 30 kg | R Art. 3(1)(12) | **EV battery — not portable** | L-category traction battery weighing more than 25 kg |
| Car starter battery | 15 kg | R Art. 3(1)(13) | **SLI battery — not portable** | Also >5 kg |
| Home/domestic energy-storage unit | 4 kg | R Art. 3(1)(9) + recital (15) | **Industrial — not portable** | Recital (15): energy storage in private or domestic environments is industrial. Under the Directive the same unit would likely have been portable (sealed, hand-carryable, neither industrial nor automotive) — a real change of outcome |
| Forklift traction battery | 500 kg | R Art. 3(1)(14) | **Industrial** | Designed for industrial use; also >5 kg |
| Rail/waterborne/aviation/off-road machinery traction battery | any | R recital (15) + Art. 3(1)(14) | **Industrial** | Recital (15) keeps these in the industrial category |
| Button cell in a watch | <0.01 kg | R Art. 3(1)(9), (10) | Portable; portable battery of general use | Button cell is a listed common format |

---

## 6. Red-line change log for the classification procedure

1. **Legal basis.** Replace "Article 3(3) of Directive 2006/66/EC" with "Article 3(1)(9) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542" as the current basis; retain the Directive citation only in the legacy branch (Step 6) and label it as historical.
2. **Terminology.** Replace "portable battery or accumulator" with "portable battery" throughout the current-law sections. "Accumulator" is not a defined term in the Regulation; retain it only in the legacy/Directive section.
3. **Criterion 2.** Delete "can be hand-carried" from the current-law test; insert "weighs 5 kg or less (inclusive)". Add a mandatory weighing record.
4. **Criterion 3.** Replace "is neither an industrial battery or accumulator nor an automotive battery or accumulator" with the four-part Regulation test: "not designed specifically for industrial use and is neither an electric vehicle battery, an LMT battery, nor an SLI battery".
5. **New definitions.** Insert Art. 3(1)(11) (LMT), 3(1)(12) (EV), 3(1)(13) (SLI) and 3(1)(14) (industrial, including the >5 kg residual rule) as annexes to the procedure, verbatim.
6. **New rule.** Insert: "A battery weighing more than 5 kg that is not an EV, LMT or SLI battery is an industrial battery (Art. 3(1)(14))."
7. **New rule.** Insert: "A battery used for energy storage in private or domestic environments is an industrial battery (recital 15)."
8. **New rule.** Insert: "A battery that has been subject to preparation for repurposing or repurposing and is given industrial uses is an industrial battery (Art. 3(1)(14); recital 15)."
9. **Sub-category.** Insert Art. 3(1)(10) and state expressly that "portable battery of general use" is a subset of portable battery, not an alternative classification route.
10. **Boundary rule.** Insert: "A battery weighing exactly 5.00 kg is a portable battery. The threshold is inclusive."
11. **Do-not-import rule.** Insert a caution in the legacy section: "The 5 kg threshold belongs to Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 only. It must not be applied when assessing under Directive 2006/66/EC."
12. **Weighing convention.** State the convention used (e.g. battery as placed on the market, including its own casing, excluding retail packaging) and record it on each assessment; see §7.

---

## 7. Citation and interpretation notes to close before sign-off

1. **Directive examples recital number.** The recital text quoted in §1.5 is confirmed, but the recital *number* was not visible in the fetched extract. Confirm the number against OJ L 266, 26.9.2006, p. 1 before it is printed. Until then, cite it by its opening words.
2. **"Hand-carried" has no numeric equivalent.** Do not convert it to 5 kg, 2 kg or any other figure in the legacy branch; the only gloss available is the recital's "an average person could carry by hand without difficulty".
3. **Weighing convention.** Neither text states how the 5 kg mass is measured (with or without retail packaging, with or without an installed housing). The cited texts are silent; adopt and document a convention (battery as placed on the market, including its own casing) and obtain legal confirmation before relying on it for a borderline product.
4. **"Designed specifically for industrial use" (Regulation) vs. "designed for exclusively industrial or professional uses" (Directive).** The two formulas are not interchangeable, and the Regulation gives no definition of "industrial use" beyond Art. 3(1)(14) and recital (15)'s non-exhaustive list (industrial activities, communication infrastructure, agricultural activities, generation and distribution of electric energy). Document the design-intent evidence (technical documentation, intended-use statement, marketing) for every borderline professional product.
5. **Transitional provisions.** Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 applies from 18 February 2024 and repeals Directive 2006/66/EC with effect from that date, subject to the staged application dates and transitional provisions in the Regulation's final articles. The *definitions* are governed by the Regulation from that date; where the procedure also covers obligations that continue to apply post-repeal, verify the applicable transitional article before relying on the Directive's wording for anything other than classification history.
6. **Version control.** Quote Art. 3(1)(9) from the consolidated text `02023R1542` and note the consolidation date on the procedure, so that later amendments and corrigenda can be tracked. The definition is unchanged between the 28.07.2023 consolidation and the 2026-08-13 consolidation as fetched.
7. **Answer to the "Article 3 / Annex I" question.** The Directive's classification definition sits in **Article 3(3)**, not in an Annex; cite it there.

The UN page for the Universal Declaration of Human Rights gives the date as: **10 December 1948**.

SOURCE (the page the constraint names)
URL: https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights
Page title: "Universal Declaration of Human Rights" (un.org > About Us > UDHR)

"The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights. Drafted by representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions of the world, the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations."

The ask uses the page's own verb — "proclaimed ... by the UN General Assembly in Paris." The page's preamble text ("The General Assembly, Proclaims this Universal Declaration of Human Rights ...") is the Declaration's own proclamation clause and carries no date; the date-bearing statement is the introductory paragraph quoted above.

CORROBORATION ACROSS OTHER OFFICIAL UN PAGES (all agree; no date conflict)
- https://www.un.org/en/about-us/udhr/history-of-the-declaration — "By its resolution 217 A (III) of 10 December 1948, the General Assembly, meeting in Paris, adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights with eight nations abstaining from the vote but none dissenting." (Also: "adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948".)
- https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/human-rights — "... the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 by General Assembly resolution 217 A (III) ..."

Some pages say "proclaimed," others "adopted." Both refer to the same act on the same day, and every official UN page cited above gives 10 December 1948. The only other December date in the record is 9 December 1948, which appears solely as the first day of General Assembly consideration of the Third Committee report (180th–183rd meetings, 9–10 December); it is not the date given for proclamation/adoption on any page and must not be reported.

SCOPE / CAVEATS RECORDED
- Source is the English-language un.org page, current live version, as fetched on the timestamp above. Other language versions of the UDHR pages render the date in local form (e.g. "10 de diciembre de 1948") but denote the same day.
- The answer is the date the page states, not an independently re-derived historical date; the two happen to coincide.

ONE-LINE RESULT
Proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A), per https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights.

question: Y17
answer:
# Answer: UDHR Article 26(1) — free stages vs. compulsory stage

## 1. Grounding passage (verbatim)

Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 26, paragraph (1), English text as reproduced by the UN (un.org/en/udhrbook/index.shtml), the UN PDF (un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2021/03/udhr.pdf), OHCHR's poster edition (ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/Publications/Posteren.pdf), and the Council of Europe / Compasito full reprint (rm.coe.int/universal-declaration-of-human-rights-in-full-/1680b6cbd7):

> "Everyone has the right to education. Education shall be free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages. Elementary education shall be compulsory. Technical and professional education shall be made generally available and higher education shall be equally accessible to all on the basis of merit."

All four sources are byte-identical on the operative sentences; there is no variant wording to reconcile.

## 2. Clause-by-clause extraction of the stage names

| Clause (verbatim) | Obligation | Stage(s) named (exact wording from the passage) |
|---|---|---|
| "Education shall be free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages." | FREE | elementary; fundamental (the passage phrase is "elementary and fundamental stages") |
| "Elementary education shall be compulsory." | COMPULSORY | elementary |
| "Technical and professional education shall be made generally available ..." | generally available — NOT stated free, NOT stated compulsory | technical and professional |
| "... and higher education shall be equally accessible to all on the basis of merit." | equally accessible on the basis of merit — NOT stated free, NOT stated compulsory | higher |

## 3. Ask 1 — which stages of education must be free

**Answer (exact stage wording from the passage): the elementary and fundamental stages.**

Value: "elementary and fundamental stages"

Basis: the free clause names precisely two stages — "elementary" and "fundamental" — and attaches the modality "shall be free" to them. The qualifier "at least" means these two are a floor: the passage does not forbid free provision at other stages, but it does not require it either. Therefore the answer to "which stages must be free" is exactly the two named stages, no more and no less.

Exclusions enforced (free ≠ accessible):
- "technical and professional education" — the passage says only "shall be made generally available"; it is NOT stated to be free.
- "higher education" — the passage says only "shall be equally accessible to all on the basis of merit"; it is NOT stated to be free.
Conflating "generally available" or "equally accessible" with "free" would misstate Article 26 and is not supported by the text.

## 4. Ask 2 — which stage must be compulsory

**Answer (exact stage wording from the passage): elementary.**

Value: "elementary"

Basis: "Elementary education shall be compulsory." This is the only occurrence of "compulsory" in Article 26, and it is attached solely to elementary education. No other stage is made compulsory by the passage: "fundamental" appears only in the free clause; "technical and professional" is only "generally available"; "higher" is only "equally accessible".

## 5. Constraint compliance (ask 3)

Both answers above use the stage names exactly as they appear in the passage — "elementary", "fundamental" (free clause: "elementary and fundamental stages") and "elementary" (compulsory clause) — with no paraphrase, substitution, or modern educational taxonomy substituted (e.g., no "primary", "basic", "secondary", or "tertiary" wording).

## 6. Results (as stated in the summary)

- Ask 1 (free stages): value = "elementary and fundamental stages", unit = (none, identifier).
- Ask 2 (compulsory stage): value = "elementary", unit = (none, identifier).

No numeric figures are asserted anywhere in this deliverable; article/paragraph numbers (Article 26(1)) are citations, not computed values, so no value can conflict with a stated bound.

question: Y18
answer:
ANSWER

The UNFCCC Convention enters into force on the NINETIETH DAY after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession — i.e., 90 days after that date.

AUTHORITY AND VERBATIM TEXT

Instrument: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted 9 May 1992, New York; opened for signature at Rio de Janeiro 4 June 1992 and at UN Headquarters until 19 June 1993.
Provision: Article 23 (Entry into Force), paragraph 1, in the Final Clauses.

Verbatim (authentic English text, UNFCCC secretariat document, https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T00:07:42Z, sha256 38a5cee8b310):

  "Article 23
   ENTRY INTO FORCE
   1. The Convention shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the
   fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession."

HISTORICAL APPLICATION (corroboration)

The fiftieth instrument of ratification was deposited on 21 December 1993; the Convention accordingly entered into force on 21 March 1994. Day-count check, applying the ordinary rule that the day of deposit is not counted and counting begins on the following day:
  - 22-31 Dec 1993 = days 1-10
  - 1-31 Jan 1994 = days 11-41
  - 1-28 Feb 1994 (1994 not a leap year) = days 42-69
  - 1-21 Mar 1994 = days 70-90
Day 90 = 21 March 1994. This confirms that "ninetieth day after the date of deposit" is computed exclusive of the deposit date, not as a 90-day period ending on day 89 or day 91.

RELATED PROVISIONS IN THE SAME ARTICLE (context, not additional answers)

  - Art. 23(2): the same ninetieth-day rule applies to each State or regional economic integration organization ratifying, accepting, approving or acceding AFTER the deposit of the fiftieth instrument — the count runs from that Party's own deposit date.
  - Art. 23(3): an instrument deposited by a regional economic integration organization is not counted as additional to those deposited by its member States (relevant to identifying which instrument is "the fiftieth").
  - Art. 24: no reservations may be made to the Convention.
  - Art. 26: the Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish texts are equally authentic, so the 90-day figure holds across all six authentic versions.

SCOPE AND DISTINCTIONS (guarding against cross-instrument error)

  - The 90-day figure is the rule of the 1992 Convention itself and is unaffected by subsequent amendments, decisions or rules of procedure; entry into force is a historical, spent event (21 March 1994) and no later instrument changes Article 23(1).
  - It is NOT the rule of the Convention's instruments: the Kyoto Protocol (Art. 25) requires 55 Parties including Annex I Parties accounting for at least 55% of 1990 CO2 emissions, and the Paris Agreement (Art. 21) requires 55 Parties accounting for at least 55% of global greenhouse gas emissions, entering into force on the THIRTIETH day after the deposit of the last such instrument. Those are 30-day (Paris) and different-threshold (Kyoto) rules and must not be substituted for the Convention's 90 days.
  - The count runs from the date of DEPOSIT of the instrument, not from signature, approval in principle, or notification.

BOTTOM LINE

90 days — the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession (UNFCCC Art. 23(1)).
cautions: The recompute vote did not run, so no figure in this answer was recomputed.
The answer gives 90 days for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y19
answer:
ANSWER

Under the Kyoto Protocol text, each Party included in Annex I must have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under the Protocol by 2005.

Controlling provision: Kyoto Protocol, Article 3, paragraph 2.

OPERATIVE TEXT (verbatim)

  'Article 3 ... 2. Each Party included in Annex I shall, by 2005, have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under this Protocol.'

  — Kyoto Protocol to the UNFCCC, adopted 11 December 1997 (FCCC/CP/1997/7/Add.1), Article 3(2).

PROVENANCE AND VERIFICATION

1. Primary text, COP-3 distribution version (https://unfccc.int/cop3/resource/docs/cop3/protocol.pdf, sha256 d884dfc86aa8): Article 3(2) appears exactly as quoted, immediately before paragraph 3 (LULUCF net changes) and paragraph 4 (1990 carbon-stock data to be provided prior to the first session of the COP/MOP), and before paragraph 7 (the 2008-2012 assigned amount).
2. Primary text, consolidated version (https://unfccc.int/files/kyoto_protocol/application/pdf/kp_consoldiated_text.pdf, sha256 ce7f4290e56b): the identical sentence appears, with the same paragraph numbering, in the consolidated text incorporating amendments. Two independent renderings of the treaty agree word-for-word, so the reading does not depend on a single transcription.
3. Corroborating decision practice: Decision 25/CP.8, 'Demonstrable progress under Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Kyoto Protocol' (New Delhi, 2002; ECOLEX record 75d881d8-83dc-4480-aca5-66dbf73f5358), recalling Article 3(2) and decisions 4/CP.5 and 22/CP.7, refers twice to 'reviewing the demonstration of progress by 2005, in accordance with Article 3, paragraph 2, of the Kyoto Protocol.' This fixes both the article number and the year independently of the treaty PDFs.

CHARACTER OF THE OBLIGATION (so the answer is not over-read)

- The Protocol sets a single explicit year, 2005, and states it as a deadline ('shall, by 2005, have made'), not a target range. No interpretation across multiple clauses is needed to fix the year.
- 'Demonstrable progress' is NOT defined quantitatively in the Protocol text. Article 3(2) is a benchmark/reporting obligation; the Protocol supplies no percentage, no emissions threshold and no prescribed indicator set. The content was elaborated in COP decisions: decision 22/CP.7 urged each Annex I Party that is also a Party to the Protocol to submit, by 1 January 2006, a report giving the basis for reviewing the demonstration of progress by 2005; decision 25/CP.8 specifies that the report contain (a) a description of domestic measures, including legal and institutional steps and domestic compliance/enforcement programmes; (b) trends in and projections of greenhouse gas emissions; (c) an evaluation of how those measures, in light of the trends and projections, will contribute to meeting the Article 3 commitments; and (d) a description of activities under Articles 10 and 11 — and requested the secretariat to synthesize the reports for the SBI's first session in 2006.
- Scope: the obligation runs to 'each Party included in Annex I' — i.e. each Annex I Party that is a Party to the Protocol. It binds Parties to the Protocol, not every Annex I Party to the UNFCCC as such; a State that had not ratified or acceded by the relevant date was not bound by Article 3(2). The obligation is distinct from, and additional to, the quantified emission limitation and reduction commitments inscribed in Annex B.
- Timing wrinkle worth flagging in any memo: the Protocol entered into force on 16 February 2005, so the Article 3(2) deadline fell in the same calendar year as entry into force. That is a real feature of the instrument, not an error in the answer, and it explains why the reporting/review machinery (report by 1 January 2006; SBI review in 2006) post-dates the 2005 benchmark.

DATES IN THE PROTOCOL THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH 2005

- 2008-2012: the first quantified emission limitation and reduction commitment period (Art. 3(1), 3(7)). This is the compliance window for the Annex B targets, not the demonstrable-progress milestone.
- One year prior to the start of the first commitment period (i.e., 2007): deadline for each Annex I Party to have in place a national system for estimating anthropogenic emissions and removals (Art. 5(1)).
- At least seven years before the end of the first commitment period: the COP/MOP must initiate consideration of commitments for subsequent periods (Art. 3(9)).
- 1990 (or the base year/period determined under Art. 3(5)): the base year for assigned amounts and for the LULUCF provisions of Art. 3(3)-(4).

CITATION FOR USE

Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, Art. 3, para. 2 (1997): 'Each Party included in Annex I shall, by 2005, have made demonstrable progress in achieving its commitments under this Protocol.' Answer to the question posed: 2005.

LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

It states only what the treaty text says: the year is 2005. It does not assert that any particular Party in fact made demonstrable progress by that date, nor does it supply a quantitative test for 'demonstrable progress', because the Protocol text contains none; any such assessment must rest on the decision guidance above and on Parties' reports and review findings.

Source basis (Paris Agreement publication page only): the page gives the Agreement as opened for signature on 22 April 2016 and as entered into force on 4 November 2016.

Day-count convention: elapsed calendar days = end date minus start date, with the start date excluded and the end date included. Thus 22 April 2016 is day 0, 23 April 2016 is day 1, and 4 November 2016 is day 196.

Month-by-month count from 22 April 2016 to 4 November 2016:
- 23–30 April: 8 days
- May: 31 days (running total 39)
- June: 30 days (69)
- July: 31 days (100)
- August: 31 days (131)
- September: 30 days (161)
- October: 31 days (192)
- 1–4 November: 4 days (196)

Total: 8 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 4 = 196 calendar days.

Day-of-year check for leap year 2016:
- Day of year for 22 April 2016 = 31 + 29 + 31 + 22 = 113.
- Day of year for 4 November 2016 = 31 + 29 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 4 = 309.

Result: 196 calendar days elapsed from 22 April 2016 to 4 November 2016. An inclusive count of both endpoint dates would be 197, but the requested elapsed-day count uses the standard exclusive-start convention, giving 196.
