question: Y21
answer:
COMPLIANCE NOTE AMENDMENT — PARIS AGREEMENT ENTRY INTO FORCE PARAMETERS (reference date 2026-11-21)

A. BOTTOM LINE

The note must drop the UNFCCC Convention figures (fiftieth instrument / ninetieth day) and use the Paris Agreement's own dual threshold in Article 21(1):

  - Party-count threshold: at least 55 Parties to the Convention
  - Emissions-share threshold: those Parties accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of total global greenhouse gas emissions
  - Interval: entry into force on the thirtieth day (30 days) after the date on which those instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession have been deposited

All three figures are identical in every authoritative text examined for the 2026-11-21 reference date; there is no version divergence to resolve. The note's current text is wrong on all three parameters, not merely on the day count.

B. THE THREE PARAMETERS, WITH SOURCE TEXT

Governing provision: Paris Agreement, Article 21(1).

Verbatim (UNFCCC booklet publication, p. 22; identical in UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113, and in the UNFCCC English text PDF):

  "1. This Agreement shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession."

Parameter table (Paris Agreement vs the Convention figures now in the note):

  | Parameter              | Convention (UNFCCC Art. 17(1)) — to be removed | Paris Agreement (Art. 21(1)) — to be used |
  |------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
  | Instrument/Party count | 50 instruments                                | at least 55 Parties to the Convention     |
  | Emissions share        | none                                          | at least an estimated 55 per cent of total global GHG emissions |
  | Interval               | ninetieth day (90 days)                       | thirtieth day (30 days)                   |
  | Trigger point          | deposit of the fiftieth instrument            | date on which both conditions are met     |

Note on the Convention column: the 'fiftieth instrument / ninetieth day' figures are UNFCCC Article 17(1) figures. They are taken from the request itself and are not drawn from the fetched source set; they are reproduced here only to identify what is being replaced. Arithmetic cross-check for internal consistency: 50th instrument deposited 21 December 1993 + 90 days = 21 March 1994 (UNFCCC entry into force), which confirms 'ninetieth day' is a Convention figure and cannot be reconciled with the Paris Agreement's 2016 dates.

C. WHICH PUBLICATION IS AUTHORITATIVE FOR 2026-11-21

The publication in force on 2026-11-21 is the Paris Agreement as registered in the United Nations Treaty Series and published by the depositary (Secretary-General of the United Nations):

  - UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113; registered ex officio 4 November 2016.
  - Certified true copy issued under C.N.92.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d of 17 March 2016; opening for signature notified by C.N.63.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d of 16 February 2016.
  - Depositary status page, Chapter XXVII.7.d, status as at 22-11-2026: entry into force 4 November 2016 'in accordance with article 21(1)'; Signatories 194, Parties 194; text: certified true copy, UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79.
  - Corroborating reproduction: UNFCCC secretariat booklet edition of the Paris Agreement (which also reproduces decision 1/CP.21, FCCC/CP/2015/10/Add.1), and the UNFCCC English text PDF. Article 21 is verbatim identical in all of these.

Version-risk assessment: no amendment to Article 21 has entered into force as at the reference date, and no fetched source shows a variant Article 21 text. Article 21(1) is in any event a spent condition (satisfied 5 October 2016), so later party-count changes cannot alter it. The 194-Party figure as at 22-11-2026 does not change the threshold; it only confirms the threshold is long satisfied.

Source-set artefact to avoid propagating: the UNFCCC English text PDF extraction shows a running head 'Article 23' immediately before the withdrawal provision; the withdrawal provision is Article 28 (correctly labelled in the booklet). Cite Article 28 if withdrawal is ever added.

Not relied on for the numbers: the EUR-Lex publication (CELEX 22016A1019(01)) appears in the source set but yielded no quoted Article 21 passage; the depositary text governs in any event. Article 29 provides that the Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish texts are equally authentic — if the note is not in English, verify against the equally authentic language version, which carries equal authority.

D. DROP-IN REPLACEMENT TEXT FOR THE NOTE

Delete the existing sentence referring to 'the fiftieth instrument' and 'the ninetieth day'. Insert:

  "Article 21(1) of the Paris Agreement provides that the Agreement 'shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.' The threshold was achieved on 5 October 2016 and the Agreement entered into force on 4 November 2016 (United Nations Treaty Series, vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113). For a State or regional economic integration organization depositing its instrument after that date, Article 21(3) provides that the Agreement enters into force for that Party on the thirtieth day after the date of deposit of its instrument."

Mandatory footnote to accompany the emissions-share figure:

  "Article 21(2) of the Paris Agreement: 'Solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1 of this Article, "total global greenhouse gas emissions" means the most up-to-date amount communicated on or before the date of adoption of this Agreement by the Parties to the Convention.' The 55 per cent share is therefore measured against data communicated on or before 12 December 2015 and is not recalculated against later inventories or later party counts. Under Article 21(4), an instrument deposited by a regional economic integration organization is not counted as additional to those deposited by its member States."

Optional sentence if the note addresses withdrawal (Article 28): a Party may withdraw at any time after three years from the date on which the Agreement entered into force for it, by written notification to the Depositary; withdrawal takes effect on expiry of one year from receipt of the notification, or a later date specified in it; a Party that withdraws from the Convention is considered also to have withdrawn from the Agreement.

E. HOW THE EMISSIONS SHARE IS DEFINED AND MEASURED (the point most often got wrong)

1. The share is not a live, rolling figure. Article 21(2) freezes the denominator: 'total global greenhouse gas emissions' means the most up-to-date amount communicated on or before the date of adoption of this Agreement (12 December 2015) by the Parties to the Convention. The note must not imply that the share is recalculated from current national inventory reports, from a base year the note selects, or from IPCC AR6 data.
2. The accounting convention is therefore: national communications / inventory data communicated by Parties to the Convention on or before 12 December 2015, as assessed by the depositary at the time the threshold was tested. The note should not assert a specific percentage figure beyond 'at least an estimated 55 per cent' unless it also cites the depositary's assessment; the treaty text itself is the safe citation.
3. No double counting: Article 21(4) — a regional economic integration organization's instrument is not counted in addition to its member States' instruments. If the note enumerates instruments, the EU instrument must not be added on top of the 27 member State instruments.
4. Article 21(2) is expressly 'solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1'. It does not govern the transparency framework under Article 13, which uses IPCC-accepted good-practice methodologies. Do not cross-reference the two.

F. INTERVAL: ARITHMETIC AND THE 21(1)/21(3) DISTINCTION

1. Interval is 30 days ('thirtieth day'), counted from the date of the triggering deposit — not 90 days. Consistency check: threshold achieved 5 October 2016; 5 October 2016 + 30 days = 4 November 2016, which matches the depositary's recorded entry into force and the booklet's narrative ('On 5 October 2016, the threshold for entry into force was achieved and the Paris Agreement entered into force on 4 November 2016'). A ninetieth-day rule would have produced 3 January 2017 and is demonstrably wrong.
2. Tense and function. For a note written on or after 4 November 2016, Article 21(1) is a historical condition, already satisfied; the note should describe it in the past tense and cite the entry into force date, rather than saying the Agreement 'shall enter into force' on satisfaction of a condition still outstanding. If the note is about a specific Party that joined later, the operative rule is Article 21(3): thirtieth day after the date of that Party's deposit. Quoting only Article 21(1) in that scenario is a substantive error even though the numbers are right.
3. Article 27: no reservations may be made. If the note discusses conditions attached by a Party, characterise them as declarations, not reservations.

G. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THE NOTE IS ISSUED

1. Confirm no occurrence of 'fiftieth', 'fiftieth instrument', 'ninetieth day' or '90 days' remains in the note in connection with the Paris Agreement.
2. Confirm the note's Paris Agreement sentence carries the dual threshold (55 Parties AND 55 per cent), not the Party count alone.
3. Confirm the emissions-share footnote citing Article 21(2) is present wherever the 55 per cent figure appears.
4. Confirm the citation resolves to UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113 (registered 4 November 2016), with C.N.92.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d as the certified-true-copy notification.
5. Confirm the note does not add the EU instrument to its member States' instruments (Article 21(4)).
6. If the note discusses withdrawal, confirm it cites Article 28 (three years / one year) and not 'Article 23'.
7. If the note is in a language other than English, verify Article 21 against that equally authentic text (Article 29).

H. SCOPE OF THIS OPINION

This is a documentary and citation-compliance determination: it states what the text in force on 2026-11-21 says and what the note must say to match it. It does not determine which publication a particular regulator or court in an unnamed jurisdiction will treat as controlling, nor does it give legal advice on the consequences of a misstatement in any specific filing. Those points turn on the jurisdiction of the compliance note, which was not specified.

question: Y22
answer:
ANSWER

Difference in calendar years = 1976 - 1975 = 1 year.

Instrument: Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space (Registration Convention), GA resolution 3235 (XXIX), annex.

1. DATES EXTRACTED FROM UNOOSA SOURCES

| Event | Date | Year | Source (UNOOSA) | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adoption by the General Assembly | 12 November 1974 | 1974 | unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/registration-convention.html | Quoted: '2280th plenary meeting, 12 November 1974.' (NOT used in the calculation) |
| Opened for signature | 14 January 1975, New York | 1975 | same page; identical text also in the UNOOSA treaty text PDF mirrored at faa.gov/.../Conv_Regi_Objects_Launched.pdf | Quoted: 'opened for signature at New York on the fourteenth day of January, one thousand nine hundred and seventy-five.' |
| Entry into force | 15 September 1976 | 1976 | unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/capacitybuilding/registrationproject/index.html + standard UNOOSA treaty-status line for this Convention | Quoted (Registration Project page): the project 'forms part of the preparations for the 50th anniversary of the entry into force of the Registration Convention in 2026' -> 2026 - 50 = 1976. Mechanism per Article VIII(3) quoted on the treaty page: 'shall enter into force ... on the deposit of the fifth such instrument.' |

2. COMPUTATION (calendar-year difference, per the requested format)

  year_opened_for_signature = 1975
  year_entry_into_force    = 1976
  difference = 1976 - 1975 = 1

Method: subtract the opening-for-signature year from the entry-into-force year, discarding months and days. This is the 'difference in calendar years' convention: it counts year boundaries crossed, not elapsed full years.

3. VERIFICATION AND DISAMBIGUATION

- Not 0: the two events fall in different calendar years (1975 vs 1976), so the difference cannot be zero.
- Not 2: using the adoption date (12 November 1974) would give 2, but the ask explicitly says 'opened for signature'. Adoption (1974), opening for signature (1975) and entry into force (1976) are three distinct events for this Convention; only the second and third enter the calculation.
- Elapsed-time reading agrees: 14 January 1975 -> 15 September 1976 is 1 year 8 months, which truncates to 1 full year. The simple-subtraction reading and the elapsed-full-years reading therefore give the same answer (1), so the result is not sensitive to which of the two 'difference in years' conventions is intended.
- Sensitivity to the exact entry-into-force date: the answer depends only on the entry-into-force YEAR being 1976. Any date from 1 January 1976 to 31 December 1976 yields the same result, so residual uncertainty about the day (15 September) does not affect the value.
- Source integrity: the opening-for-signature clause appears identically in two independently fetched copies of the UNOOSA treaty text (unoosa.org treaty page and the UNOOSA text PDF), and the 1976 entry-into-force year is corroborated by UNOOSA's own 50th-anniversary statement (2026) and by the treaty's Article VIII(3) fifth-ratification trigger.

4. CAVEAT ON GROUNDING (stated, not blocking)

The fetched excerpt of the UNOOSA treaty page did not include the treaty-status header line that prints 'Entry into force: 15 September 1976'; the entry-into-force YEAR was therefore derived from UNOOSA's 50th-anniversary statement (2026 - 50 = 1976) and corroborated by the standard UNOOSA treaty-status date. Because the ask is a calendar-year difference, and the year 1976 is established by UNOOSA's own text, the answer 1 is fully grounded.

FINAL: 1 year.

question: Y23
answer: Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the maximum breadth of the territorial sea is 12 nautical miles from the baselines: Article 3 provides that every State has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles, measured from baselines determined in accordance with the Convention. The maximum seaward limit of the contiguous zone is 24 nautical miles from the same baselines: Article 33(2) provides that the contiguous zone may not extend beyond 24 nautical miles from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured. Using the maximum territorial-sea breadth and the maximum contiguous-zone limit from the same baselines, the contiguous zone can extend farther from those baselines than the territorial sea by: 24 nautical miles − 12 nautical miles = 12 nautical miles. Thus, at the treaty maximums, the territorial sea runs from the baselines to 12 nautical miles, and the contiguous zone occupies the belt from 12 to 24 nautical miles from the baselines. The contiguous zone therefore extends 12 nautical miles farther from the baselines than the territorial sea. Answer: 12 nautical miles.

question: Y24
answer:
CONCLUSION

1. Availability of the rule at 30 nm: No. Under UNCLOS Article 10(4), the closing-line rule is available only where the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of the bay 'does not exceed 24 nautical miles.' A bay whose natural entrance points are 30 nautical miles apart fails that condition. No closing line may therefore be drawn between those two entrance points under Article 10(4), and the waters enclosed by such a line cannot be treated as internal waters by virtue of that rule.

2. Maximum entrance-point distance: 24 nautical miles. That is the ceiling stated in Article 10(4); it is a maximum, not a minimum, and the rule is available at exactly 24 nm ('does not exceed'), but not at 30 nm.

GOVERNING TEXT (UNCLOS 1982, Part II, Section 2, Article 10)

Article 10(1): 'This article relates only to bays the coasts of which belong to a single State.'

Article 10(2): 'For the purposes of this Convention, a bay is a well-marked indentation whose penetration is in such proportion to the width of its mouth as to contain land-locked waters and constitute more than a mere curvature of the coast. An indentation shall not, however, be regarded as a bay unless its area is as large as, or larger than, that of the semi-circle whose diameter is a line drawn across the mouth of that indentation.'

Article 10(3): 'For the purpose of measurement, the area of an indentation is that lying between the low-water mark around the shore of the indentation and a line joining the low-water mark of its natural entrance points. Where, because of the presence of islands, an indentation has more than one mouth, the semi-circle shall be drawn on a line as long as the sum total of the lengths of the lines across the different mouths. Islands within an indentation shall be included as if they were part of the water area of the indentation.'

Article 10(4): 'If the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of a bay does not exceed 24 nautical miles, a closing line may be drawn between these two low-water marks, and the waters enclosed thereby shall be considered as internal waters.'

Article 10(5): 'Where the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of a bay exceeds 24 nautical miles, a straight baseline of 24 nautical miles shall be drawn within the bay in such a manner as to enclose the maximum area of water that is possible with a line of that length.'

Article 10(6): 'The foregoing provisions do not apply to so-called "historic" bays, or in any case where the straight baseline system provided for in article 7 is applied.'

APPLICATION TO THE 30 NM BAY

Step 1 — Identify the operative threshold. Article 10(4) fixes the maximum distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points at 24 nautical miles. The phrase is 'does not exceed 24 nautical miles.' A distance of exactly 24 nm satisfies the condition; any distance greater than 24 nm does not.

Step 2 — Compare the facts. 30 nm > 24 nm. The condition in Article 10(4) is not met. The closing-line rule is therefore unavailable for this bay, and the bay cannot be converted into internal waters in its entirety by a line drawn between its natural entrance points.

Step 3 — State the consequence. Article 10(5) supplies the correct treatment for a bay whose entrance points exceed 24 nm: 'a straight baseline of 24 nautical miles shall be drawn within the bay in such a manner as to enclose the maximum area of water that is possible with a line of that length.' The waters on the landward side of that 24 nm line are internal waters under Article 8(1), because they lie on the landward side of the baseline of the territorial sea. The waters lying between that 24 nm line and the natural entrance points are not internal waters by virtue of Article 10; they lie seaward of the baseline and take the status otherwise applicable — territorial sea within 12 nm of the baseline or of other baselines, and EEZ or high seas beyond that, depending on the coastal State's proclaimed maritime zones.

Step 4 — Note the separate preconditions that the 30 nm figure does not displace. Even where the entrance points are 24 nm or less, Article 10(2) requires the indentation to be a 'well-marked indentation' whose penetration is in proportion to the width of its mouth so as to contain land-locked waters and constitute more than a mere curvature of the coast, and whose area is at least that of the semi-circle drawn on a line across the mouth. At 30 nm the semi-circle test in Article 10(2) is still applied — the diameter of the semi-circle is a line drawn across the mouth — but satisfying that test does not enlarge the 24 nm ceiling in Article 10(4). The semi-circle test and the 24 nm closing-line limit are cumulative, not alternative.

Step 5 — Note the exceptions. Article 10(6) disapplies Article 10 to so-called 'historic' bays and to cases where the straight-baseline system of Article 7 applies. A 30 nm bay could in principle be closed by a historic-title claim, or its waters enclosed by straight baselines under Article 7 if the geographical conditions of that article are met, but those are distinct legal bases. Neither is available merely because the bay's entrance points are 30 nm apart, and neither converts the Article 10(4) rule into a 30 nm rule.

TEXTUAL POINTS CONFIRMING THE ANSWER

- The measurement is expressly between 'the low-water marks of the natural entrance points,' matching the reviewer's description of a line drawn between low-water marks. The reviewer's geometry is therefore the geometry Article 10(4) addresses; the defect is the distance, not the endpoints.
- The figure in Article 10(4) is 24 nautical miles in every authoritative reproduction of the Convention (the UN Treaty Collection text, the UN DOALOS publication, and the UNCLOS compendium all read '24 nautical miles').
- The same 24 nm limit appears in Article 7(4) of the 1958 Convention on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone, which preceded UNCLOS and stated the same rule. The conclusion therefore does not turn on whether the reviewer had UNCLOS 1982 or the earlier convention in mind.
- Article 5 confirms that the ordinary baseline is the low-water line along the coast, which is consistent with Article 10's use of low-water marks; Article 10 is a special rule displacing the ordinary baseline for juridical bays that satisfy its conditions.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE REVIEWER

The reviewer is right about the form of the rule — a closing line between the low-water marks of natural entrance points, with the enclosed waters becoming internal waters — but wrong about the distance. That rule exists in UNCLOS Article 10(4) and its maximum entrance-point distance is 24 nautical miles. At 30 nautical miles the rule is unavailable; the bay must instead be treated under Article 10(5) by drawing a 24 nautical mile straight baseline within the bay so as to enclose the maximum possible area.

question: Y25
answer:
FINDING (Ask 1 — verdict)

No. The passage of the supplied text that establishes absolute liability — Article II of the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects (London/Moscow/Washington, 29 March 1972) — contains no monetary cap. It states no sum, ceiling, formula, index, per-incident or per-claim limit, and it does not refer out to any provision that supplies one. The word 'compensation' appears with no amount attached to it.

VERBATIM PASSAGE RELIED ON (Ask 2 — basis)

Article II, as it appears in the supplied public text (UNOOSA treaty page; FAA reproduction of the Convention; UN Juridical Yearbook 1971, ch. IV; Lovdata treaty database):

    "Article II
    A launching State shall be absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight."

Textual note (recorded so the record is not silently cleaned up): the UNOOSA HTML rendering of the same article reads "...or to aircraft flight", omitting "in". That is a rendering/transcription artifact. Every other supplied source — the FAA PDF, the UN Juridical Yearbook PDF, the Lovdata text, and the Springer commentary quoting Article II — reads "aircraft in flight", which is also the reading in Article IV(1)(a) of the same sources. The omission does not affect the answer: with or without "in", the sentence states liability and no amount.

WHAT THE PASSAGE DOES SAY ABOUT LIABILITY (Ask 2 — restatement, confined to the passage)

Element by element, Article II states and states only the following:

1. Who is liable — "A launching State". The bearer of the obligation is the launching State (the term is defined elsewhere in the instrument, in Article I; that definition is not part of this passage and is not restated here).

2. What the standard of liability is — "shall be absolutely liable". Liability is absolute: it is triggered by the causal connection alone. The passage attaches no fault requirement, no negligence requirement, no due-diligence standard, and no burden on the claimant to prove wrongful conduct. This is the respect in which it differs from Article III of the same text, which imposes liability "only if the damage is due to its fault or the fault of persons for whom it is responsible" for damage occurring elsewhere than on the surface of the earth.

3. What the obligation is — "to pay compensation". The obligation is a payment obligation. The passage names the obligation but fixes no quantum.

4. For what — "for damage caused by its space object". The damage must be caused by the launching State's space object. "Damage" is not quantified or capped in this passage.

5. Where — "on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight". The absolute standard is geographically and materially bounded: it governs damage on the surface of the earth and damage to aircraft in flight. Article IV(1)(a) of the same text repeats the standard for the third-State case ("their liability to the third State shall be absolute") when the damage is on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight.

What the passage does not say, stated expressly because it is the point of the question:

- It does not state a maximum, ceiling, cap, or any figure in any currency.
- It does not state a formula, index, or method for computing an amount.
- It does not incorporate a limit by reference to any other article or instrument.
- It does not condition payment on a fund, insurance, registration, or budgetary appropriation.
- It does not create a presumption, rebuttable or otherwise, as to amount.
- It does not use the words 'limit', 'maximum', 'up to', 'not exceeding', or their equivalents.

CONTEXT EXPRESSLY MARKED AS OUTSIDE THE PASSAGE (not part of the answer to Ask 2)

For completeness of the file, and flagged as context only because the request confines the restatement to the absolute-liability passage:

- Article VI(1) of the same text provides for exoneration from absolute liability to the extent the launching State establishes that the damage resulted from gross negligence or an act or omission done with intent to cause damage by the claimant State or its represented persons. That is a defence to liability, not a cap on amount.
- Article XII of the same text provides that compensation "shall be determined in accordance with international law and the principles of justice and equity, in order to provide such reparation ... as will restore the person ... to the condition which would have existed if the damage had not occurred" — a restoration standard, again with no figure.
- Article XIII addresses the currency of payment; Article XVIII establishes the Claims Commission. None of these supplies a monetary ceiling.
- A secondary commentary in the supplied materials (Springer, on the Liability Convention) states the same conclusion in terms: the Convention "deliberately does not provide for any maximum limit to damages". This is corroboration only; the finding above rests on the primary text.

SCOPE AND LIMITS OF THIS FINDING

This is a finding about the text as supplied. It answers the question 'does this passage state a monetary cap' and 'what does this passage say about liability'. It does not opine on whether a tribunal might in practice arrive at a bounded figure, on how 'damage' or 'launching State' are to be construed in a particular fact pattern, or on the law of any jurisdiction applying the Convention. Those would be questions of application, and would require the relevant instruments and facts to be put in evidence.

LEGAL ANALYSIS — MINIMUM NOTICE PERIOD FOR DENUNCIATION/WITHDRAWAL

1. IDENTIFICATION OF THE SUPPLIED TEXT (Ask 1 — constraint)

The supplied UN treaty text is the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, adopted 23 May 1969 (UN Doc. A/CONF.39/27; in force 27 January 1980; UNTS vol. 1155, p. 331, No. I-18232). The instrument is identified by three independent markers in the supplied pages: (a) the A/CONF.39/27 conference document carries the Convention's own article numbering and text (Arts. 26–30, 42, 55–57, 65–66); (b) the UNTS vol. 1155, No. I-18232 printing reproduces the same articles with the same wording, confirming the authentic published text; and (c) the depositary handbook (treaties.un.org/doc/source/publications/thb/english.pdf) cites 'article 56 of the Vienna Convention 1969' by name and restates the same rule.

2. THE OPERATIVE PROVISION

Article 56 — 'Denunciation of or withdrawal from a treaty containing no provision regarding termination, denunciation or withdrawal'

Paragraph 1 establishes the threshold question — whether denunciation or withdrawal is available at all where the treaty is silent:
  '1. A treaty which contains no provision regarding its termination and which does not provide for denunciation or withdrawal is not subject to denunciation or withdrawal unless:
  (a) it is established that the parties intended to admit the possibility of denunciation or withdrawal; or
  (b) a right of denunciation or withdrawal may be implied by the nature of the treaty.'

Paragraph 2 states the notice period:
  '2. A party shall give not less than twelve months' notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under paragraph 1.'

3. ANSWER (Ask 2 — value)

Minimum notice period: TWELVE MONTHS (12 months).

The operative words are 'not less than twelve months' notice'. Twelve months is therefore a floor, not a fixed term: a party may give longer notice, but not shorter. The notice is of the party's 'intention to denounce or withdraw', and it runs from the giving of notice; the Convention sets no separate rule here for when the twelve-month clock starts beyond the act of notification itself (contrast Art. 65(2), below).

4. WHY THE CROSS-REFERENCE 'UNDER PARAGRAPH 1' IS THE RIGHT HOOK

The question asks for the period 'under paragraph 1'. Article 56 is structured so that paragraph 1 defines the class of treaties and the conditions in which denunciation/withdrawal is available, and paragraph 2 attaches the twelve-month notice requirement to a denunciation/withdrawal 'under paragraph 1'. The quoted text is unambiguous on this point and no inference or calculation is required. The 1966 ILC draft articles (A/CN.4/199, draft Art. 53(2)) carry the identical sentence, confirming that the twelve-month figure is the settled drafting outcome and not a transcription artifact.

5. SCOPE CAVEATS A REVIEWER SHOULD CARRY WITH THE FIGURE

(a) Article 56 is a residual rule. It governs only where the treaty itself is silent on termination, denunciation or withdrawal. If the treaty in the file contains its own withdrawal clause, that clause supplies the notice period and Art. 56(2) does not apply — Art. 54(a) VCLT permits termination or withdrawal 'in conformity with the provisions of the treaty'. The twelve-month figure answers the question as posed ('under paragraph 1'), i.e. for the Art. 56 case.

(b) Article 54(b) is a separate route — withdrawal at any time by consent of all the parties — to which no notice period attaches.

(c) Article 65(2) is NOT the notice period and must not be confused with it. That provision sets a three-month waiting period, except in cases of special urgency, after receipt of a notification of a claim before the notifying party may carry out the proposed measure. It is a procedural cooling-off period for invoking invalidity/termination/suspension grounds, not the Art. 56(2) notice of intention to denounce. Likewise, the twelve-month period in Art. 66 is the outer limit for triggering the conciliation procedure under Art. 65(3), not a notice period.

(d) The depositary handbook's summary is consistent and may be cited as corroboration: 'In the case of a treaty that is silent on withdrawal or denunciation, by giving at least 12 months' notice... (see article 56 of the Vienna Convention 1969).'

6. VERIFICATION

- Text quoted verbatim from two independent reproductions in the supplied set (A/CONF.39/27 and UNTS vol. 1155, No. I-18232), which agree word for word.
- Figure stated in the answer (12 months) equals the figure in the quoted operative sentence; no rounding, conversion or computation applied.
- No other figure appearing in this analysis (3 months, Art. 65(2); 12 months, Art. 66) is presented as the answer, and each is expressly labelled as a distinct procedural period, so the deliverable contains no internally inconsistent threshold.

question: Y27
answer:
Legal basis and calculation:

Article II of the Optional Protocol to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations concerning the Compulsory Jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice (Vienna, 24 April 1963) provides that the parties concerned may agree to have recourse to a conciliation commission; that the Commission shall be constituted within two months after the date on which one party has notified the other of its intention to have recourse to conciliation; and that the Commission shall make its recommendations within five months after its appointment.

The request asks only for the sum of the two stated periods: the stated two-month period and the stated five-month period.

2 months + 5 months = 7 months.

The result is not a deadline measured from notification of the dispute. The two-month period runs from notification of intention to have recourse to conciliation, while the five-month period runs from the appointment of the Commission. The addition is therefore purely arithmetic and yields 7 months. No other period (such as any period for the President of the International Court of Justice to appoint members if the Commission is not constituted) is added.

Note: The Protocol's two-month period is expressly the period within which the Commission is to be constituted after notification of intention to have recourse to conciliation; the request's shorthand description of it as the period 'for agreeing to adopt a conciliation procedure' does not alter the stated duration of two months.
